how-to/design-substrate-infrastructure:
Design your infrastructure for Agent Substrate on GKE

Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) lets you scale Agent Substrate on GKE clusters to support high-concurrency AI agentic workloads while minimizing idle compute costs. By combining dedicated system infrastructure node pools with custom ComputeClasses and capacity buffers, you can isolate critical system components, automate hardware fallback across Compute Engine machine series, and keep standby Worker capacity warm.

Read this document to right-size your GKE cluster components, isolate system infrastructure and database node pools, configure automated node provisioning for WorkerPool resources, and plan for cluster maintenance and upgrades. This document is for platform administrators who provision and manage Agent Substrate on GKE infrastructure.

Before you begin

Before you configure your cluster infrastructure for scale, ensure that your environment meets the following requirements:

  • GKE cluster mode and version: you must use a GKE Standard cluster in which both the control plane and the node pools run version 1.37 or later. GKE Autopilot clusters aren't supported for Agent Substrate on GKE.
  • Agent Substrate on GKE installation: you must have an existing Agent Substrate on GKE installation or plan to install Agent Substrate on GKE with system infrastructure node isolation enabled. For installation steps, see Install Agent Substrate on GKE.

Right-size your Agent Substrate cluster

Size your cluster for peak concurrency and peak resume rates rather than averages. Worker nodes must hold the maximum number of Actors running at the same time, and the system infrastructure components and storage paths must keep up with the fastest rate of Actor resumes and suspends.

Estimate your workload peaks

If you don't have production measurements, then estimate your peak concurrency and resume rate from your total registered Actor count (total_actors), the average fraction of Actors running concurrently (average_active_fraction), your traffic burst multiplier (burst_factor), and the average duration that an Actor stays active per turn (average_seconds_active_per_resume):

peak_running_actors = total_actors × average_active_fraction × burst_factor
peak_resume_rate    = peak_running_actors / average_seconds_active_per_resume

For example, if you have 100,000 total Actors with 10% active on average (10,000 Actors) and a burst factor of two, then your cluster must support 20,000 peak running Actors. If each Actor runs for an average of 100 seconds before suspending, then sustaining that peak requires 200 resumes per second and 200 suspends per second.

Agent Substrate on GKE doesn't suspend idle Actors automatically; your application or orchestrator must trigger suspension.

Size the data plane

This section covers best practices for sizing the data plane, including Worker Pods, GKE nodes, snapshot bandwidth, and the atelet node agent.

Calculate Worker Pods and GKE nodes

Each Worker Pod in a WorkerPool hosts multiple Actors. A Worker can accept a new Actor while it hosts fewer Actors than the limit set by the --max-actors flag on the ateworker container (default 1000) and has enough remaining CPU and memory capacity to fit the ActorTemplate limits. For more information about how Worker limits interact with Actor limits, see the open source Right-sizing resources in the Agent Substrate API guide.

Calculate the required number of Worker Pods with 20% available scheduling capacity (the 0.8 factor):

slots_per_worker = min(max_actors, worker_memory / actor_memory, worker_cpu / actor_cpu)
total_workers    = peak_running_actors / (slots_per_worker × 0.8)

In this formula, the max_actors variable defaults to 1000 (configured by the --max-actors flag). Subtract the memory that the Worker reserves for its own process from the worker_memory value. For microVM WorkerPool resources, add the per-Actor virtual machine monitor (VMM) memory overhead reported by the Worker to the actor_memory value, because placement counts that overhead against Worker capacity.

With one Worker Pod per node, the number of Workers equals the number of GKE worker nodes. Don't allocate 100% of a node's allocatable CPU and memory to the Worker Pod; leave capacity on each node for the atelet DaemonSet (in the ate-system namespace) and GKE system daemons. GKE Standard supports up to 65,000 nodes per cluster and up to 512 Pods per node. The default maximum is 110 Pods per node (configurable with the --max-pods-per-node flag), and large clusters have additional requirements.

Size snapshot bandwidth and node disks

Each Actor suspend writes a snapshot to the local node disk under the /var/lib/ate directory path. In SYNCHRONOUS mode, the atelet agent uploads the snapshot to Cloud Storage before the suspend operation returns. In ASYNCHRONOUS mode, the atelet agent schedules the upload to Cloud Storage after a delay of approximately the --snapshot-upload-delay flag value (default 5m) from when the snapshot is taken. Agent Substrate caches the latest snapshot on the node for the period configured in the --snapshot-detach-delay flag, which defaults to a value of 30m. An Actor that resumes within that window schedules onto the same node and restores from the local disk instead of downloading the snapshot from Cloud Storage.

Estimate your uncompressed snapshot size (snapshot_size) as the ActorTemplate memory limit plus any data written to the writable root file system or durable directories. Sparse file handling and zstd compression reduce the compressed snapshot size (compressed_snapshot_size) transferred to and from Cloud Storage, where Agent Substrate stores up to two snapshots per Actor (the previous snapshot and the in-progress snapshot):

  • Peak Cloud Storage bandwidth (each direction): peak_resume_rate × compressed_snapshot_size
  • Peak node disk write throughput per node: 2 × peak_resume_rate × snapshot_size / total_nodes (both resume downloads and suspend checkpoints write to the node disk).

The default 100 GiB hyperdisk-balanced boot disk in GKE provides 3,600 IOPS and 290 MiB/s of throughput (default performance scales with disk size), which can limit snapshot operations under heavy guest I/O. When you create worker node pools, either mount a dedicated disk at the /var/lib/ate/snapshots directory path or increase boot disk performance by using the --boot-disk-provisioned-iops and --boot-disk-provisioned-throughput flags with the gcloud container node-pools create command.

Check Security Token Service quota

Each snapshot transfer to or from Cloud Storage requires a token scoped to the Actor, which the ate-api-server component requests from the Security Token Service (STS) API. The ate-api-server component makes up to one STS request per Actor every 20 to 40 minutes (typically on the first resume in that window) and reuses the token until 20 minutes before expiration.

The STS Exchange token global requests quota defaults to 6,000 requests per project per minute and is shared with Workload Identity Federation for GKE:

  • Required STS quota (requests per minute): estimate as up to 60 times the peak rate of resumes for Actors whose last snapshot transfer was more than 20 minutes ago, plus capacity for Workload Identity Federation for GKE. If you don't know that rate, use the 60 × peak_resume_rate formula as a fallback. For example, 200 resumes per second requires up to 12,000 requests per minute.
  • How to increase quota: request a quota increase on the Quotas & System Limits page in Google Cloud console. Snapshot transfers work without the Security Token Service API enabled in your project, but you must enable the API for the quota to appear on the Quotas & System Limits page. For more information, see Quota for the Exchange Token API in Security Token Service in the Workload Identity Federation for GKE documentation.

Tune the atelet node agent

The atelet DaemonSet runs one Pod per worker node to restore and checkpoint Actors. In each atelet Pod, the objectstore-plugin container compresses and transfers snapshots to and from Cloud Storage.

The following table describes key sizing settings for the atelet and objectstore-plugin containers:

Setting Default Sizing guidance
atelet and objectstore-plugin container CPU and memory Requests: 50 mCPU, 128 MiB memory; no limits Configure Burstable QoS without memory limits by omitting memory limits on both containers, because hitting a memory limit stops the node agent and halts all resumes on the node. Raise CPU and memory requests to match measured peak usage on a full node at your peak resume rate so Worker Pods don't consume resources needed by the atelet agent.
--upload-memory-budget flag (objectstore-plugin container) and --snapshot-upload-workers flag (atelet container) 512 MiB budget; 2 upload workers

To prevent concurrent snapshot uploads from queuing on multi-Actor nodes with high suspend rates, do the following:

  • Increase the value of the --upload-memory-budget flag (and set the objectstore-plugin container memory request higher than this budget).
  • Increase the value of the --snapshot-upload-workers flag.
--drain-timeout flag and terminationGracePeriodSeconds field 5 minutes (--drain-timeout flag); 330 seconds (terminationGracePeriodSeconds field) Controls how long the atelet agent finishes in-flight restores and snapshot uploads when its Pod stops during a node drain or upgrade. If you increase the value of the --drain-timeout flag for large snapshots, then also increase the value of the terminationGracePeriodSeconds field on the atelet DaemonSet so the kubelet agent doesn't stop the atelet agent before uploads finish.

Size system infrastructure components and the database

For stateless system component Deployments in the ate-system namespace that scale horizontally, estimate the required replica count with 35% available capacity (the 0.65 factor) plus one spare replica (+ 1) to tolerate node disruptions:

replicas = ceil(peak_load / (capacity_per_replica × 0.65)) + 1

Horizontal scaling stops improving throughput after a shared dependency (such as PostgreSQL CPU or connection limits) reaches capacity. Size your system infrastructure components and database together. For more information about component flags, see the open source operator install guide.

The following table describes resource and scaling rules for each system infrastructure component:

Component QoS and resource rules Scaling and connection tuning
Ingress router (atenet-router) Configure Guaranteed QoS: set matching CPU and memory requests and limits so the Go runtime aligns its thread count with the container CPU budget. Scale replicas horizontally based on peak ingress requests per second, mTLS overhead, and request payload sizes.
API server (ate-api-server) Configure Guaranteed QoS: set matching CPU and memory requests and limits so the Go runtime aligns its thread count with the container CPU budget. Scale replicas based on peak resume and suspend cycles per second (approximately 4 ms of CPU per resume and suspend cycle) and ingress request lookup load. Explicitly set the ateapi.postgres.poolMaxConns setting. Each replica opens up to poolMaxConns + 6 database connections, and the sum across all replicas must stay less than the PostgreSQL max_connections setting.
Database (PostgreSQL) Configure Burstable QoS with guaranteed memory: set memory requests equal to limits to lock the shared_buffers cache in memory and help prevent out-of-memory (OOM) eviction. Omit CPU limits when running on a dedicated ate-postgres node so kernel CPU throttling doesn't slow down checkpoint and autovacuum bursts. Scale this single-instance StatefulSet vertically. Provision enough CPU to stay at less than 80% utilization at peak load, enough RAM to cache the Actor table (with the shared_buffers parameter set to approximately 25% of memory), and an SSD-backed StorageClass set at installation time with the ateapi.postgres.storageClass setting (for example, the dynamic-rwo StorageClass on C4 or N4, or the premium-rwo StorageClass on C3 or N2). Increase the max_connections parameter in the postgres-config ConfigMap (the postgresql.conf file) to fit all ate-api-server replicas.
Egress proxy (atenet-egress) Resource rules: set a CPU request of 512 mCPU (limit 8 vCPUs) and a memory request of 512 MiB (limit 1 GiB). Increase requests and limits if outbound Actor traffic experiences increased latency. Scale replicas horizontally based on Actor outbound request traffic.
Worker controller (ate-controller) Resource rules: keep at one replica (no leader election). Set CPU and memory requests based on peak usage during large WorkerPool scale-out events. If new Worker Pods take too long to register in large fleets, then increase the value of the --worker-sync-concurrency flag (default 2).
Certificate controller (podcertificate-controller) Resource rules: runs in the podcertificate-controller-system namespace to sign mTLS certificates for new Worker Pods before they can accept Actors. For fleets of thousands of Workers, increase the values of the podcert.workersPerSigner setting (default 0, which keeps the manifest default of 1 worker per signer), the --kube-api-qps flag (default 5), and the --kube-api-burst flag (default 10).
Identity provider (ate-idp-server) Resource rules: serves the OpenID Connect (OIDC) discovery document and JSON Web Key Set (JWKS) in the ate-system namespace for verifying Actor JSON Web Tokens (JWTs). Set CPU and memory requests based on peak JWKS query volume. Scale replicas horizontally if relying parties query the JWKS endpoint at high request rates without caching keys.
Credential provider (k8s-credential-provider) Resource rules: runs in the ate-system namespace when Kubernetes Secret credential injection is enabled. Set CPU and memory requests based on outbound credential-injection volume. Scale replicas horizontally based on the rate of outbound Actor requests that require Kubernetes Secret credential injection at the atenet-egress proxy.

Isolate system infrastructure and worker node pools

In production clusters, high-churn Actor scheduling and snapshot traffic on worker nodes can compete with system infrastructure components for CPU, memory, and disk I/O. Separate your GKE cluster into three distinct node pool tiers:

  • Database node pool (ate-postgres label): a dedicated node pool for the PostgreSQL StatefulSet, which stores all Actor and Worker metadata.
  • System infrastructure node pool (ate-system-infra label): a dedicated node pool for the remaining system infrastructure services (the atenet-router, ate-api-server, atenet-egress, ate-controller, ate-idp-server, and k8s-credential-provider components).
  • Worker node pools (WorkerPool): dynamically scaled node pools managed by GKE custom ComputeClasses and GKE capacity buffers to host active Actor sandboxes.

You can isolate the database and system infrastructure components onto dedicated nodes when you install Agent Substrate on GKE by using the cordonSystemInfraComponents setting (or the --cordon-system-infra-components flag). Before you install, you must create both node pools with the required labels and NoSchedule taints:

# 1. Create the dedicated PostgreSQL node pool
gcloud container node-pools create ate-postgres-pool \
    --cluster=CLUSTER_NAME \
    --location=LOCATION \
    --node-locations=POSTGRES_ZONE \
    --machine-type=POSTGRES_MACHINE_TYPE \
    --num-nodes=1 \
    --node-labels=ate.dev/workloadType=ate-postgres \
    --node-taints=ate.dev/workloadType=ate-postgres:NoSchedule

# 2. Create the dedicated system infrastructure node pool
gcloud container node-pools create ate-system-infra-pool \
    --cluster=CLUSTER_NAME \
    --location=LOCATION \
    --machine-type=SYSTEM_INFRA_MACHINE_TYPE \
    --num-nodes=2 \
    --node-labels=ate.dev/workloadType=ate-system-infra \
    --node-taints=ate.dev/workloadType=ate-system-infra:NoSchedule

Replace the following:

  • CLUSTER_NAME: the name of your GKE Standard cluster.
  • LOCATION: the Compute Engine zone or region of your cluster's control plane.
  • POSTGRES_ZONE: a single Compute Engine zone for the single-replica PostgreSQL StatefulSet. For a regional cluster, specify one zone within the cluster's region so that the node pool provisions a single node in the zone where the StatefulSet's persistent disk will be created. For a zonal cluster, specify the cluster's zone.
  • POSTGRES_MACHINE_TYPE: the Compute Engine machine type sized for your PostgreSQL instance.
  • SYSTEM_INFRA_MACHINE_TYPE: the Compute Engine machine type sized for your system infrastructure components (for example, the c3-standard-8 machine type).

In a regional cluster, the --num-nodes flag applies per zone (for example, setting the --num-nodes=2 flag across three zones creates six nodes total). To place the ate-system-infra-pool node pool in specific zones, add the --node-locations flag.

If you enable the cordonSystemInfraComponents setting during installation and either node pool is missing, the corresponding system Pods remain in the Pending state.

Automate hardware targeting using custom ComputeClasses

GKE custom ComputeClasses let you define prioritized lists of Compute Engine machine series for your WorkerPool nodes and automatically fall back to secondary machine series if a zone experiences resource unavailability.

Select Compute Engine machine series by runtime

Configure a separate ComputeClass for each sandbox runtime:

  • MicroVM runtime (Cloud Hypervisor): set the enableNestedVirtualization: true field in your ComputeClass priorities and target x86 Compute Engine machine series that support nested virtualization (such as N4, C3, C4, or N2), or use x86 bare-metal machine types, which run KVM natively and don't require the enableNestedVirtualization field. Arm-based VMs and machine series listed in Nested virtualization restrictions aren't supported.
  • gVisor runtime: target general-purpose or compute-optimized x86 Compute Engine machine series (such as N4, C3, C4, or N2) without nested virtualization enabled. Machine series that run on mixed CPU microarchitectures (such as E2) and Arm-based VMs aren't supported for Agent Substrate on GKE. All WorkerPool resources that an ActorTemplate selects must share the same CPU architecture.

For a detailed comparison, see Select a sandbox runtime.

Required ComputeClass rules for Agent Substrate

When you create a ComputeClass for Agent Substrate on GKE worker nodes, follow these rules:

  • Use node-based ComputeClasses: don't use Pod-based billing (the podFamily field), which doesn't support nested virtualization.
  • Don't set the nodePoolConfig.sandbox.type: microvm field: that setting enables the Kata runtime for GKE Sandbox on Pod-based workloads and applies a sandbox.gke.io/runtime=microvm taint that prevents Agent Substrate on GKE Workers from scheduling. Agent Substrate on GKE manages its own microVM runtime and requires only Compute Engine nested virtualization on standard Container-Optimized OS (cos_containerd image type) nodes.

  • Configure Linux kernel sysctl settings for high sandbox density: if a worker node runs more than approximately 800 concurrent sandboxes, you must increase the Linux kernel limits for file system monitoring (fs.inotify.* parameters) and for the Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) neighbor table (net.ipv4.neigh.default.gc_thresh* parameters). The installer applies these settings only to clusters that it creates. When you configure custom ComputeClasses (by using the priorityDefaults.nodeSystemConfig.linuxNodeConfig.sysctls field) or pre-create worker node pools (by using the --system-config-from-file flag), apply the following sysctl values yourself:

    • fs.inotify.max_user_instances: 65536
    • fs.inotify.max_user_watches: 1048576
    • net.ipv4.neigh.default.gc_thresh1: 4096
    • net.ipv4.neigh.default.gc_thresh2: 16384
    • net.ipv4.neigh.default.gc_thresh3: 32768

    For more information about configuring node sysctl parameters, see Sysctl configuration options.

Choose a scale-up pattern for microVM WorkerPool resources

MicroVM Worker Pods request the ate.dev/kvm: 1 extended resource, which is advertised by the atelet device plugin only after a node boots and the atelet agent starts. Because GKE node auto-provisioning doesn't see the ate.dev/kvm extended resource on unprovisioned node templates, a pending microVM Worker Pod can't trigger GKE to auto-create a new node pool from zero replicas on its own. However, if a node pool already has at least one running node, GKE can scale that node pool up.

The following table compares the supported patterns for scaling microVM WorkerPool resources on GKE:

Pattern How it works Scales to 0 nodes? Multi-priority fallback for resource unavailability? Best used when
Auto-created pools with the minimumCapacity field Sets the nodePoolAutoCreation.enabled: true and minimumCapacity.targetNodeCount: 1 fields with explicit machineType priorities. No (keeps 1 warm node running) Only at initial provisioning for the class-level minimumCapacity field; mid-burst fallback requires setting the minimumCapacity.targetNodeCount: 1 field on each fallback entry in the spec.priorities[] field (keeping 1 warm node per priority) You want automated node pool creation and always keep at least 1 worker node running.
Auto-created pools with capacity buffers Combines the nodePoolAutoCreation.enabled: true field with an active or standby CapacityBuffer whose PodTemplate omits the ate.dev/kvm extended resource. Suspends to standby (for example, approximately 8% of running compute cost on a c3-standard-4 node with a default 100 GiB boot disk) Yes (buffer placeholders trigger node auto-provisioning fallback across priorities) You want fast burst scaling (1 to 4 seconds active, or 20 to 35 seconds to resume standby nodes and 50 to 85 seconds until new Workers are ready) with low idle cost.
Pre-created 0-node pools with node-template labels Pre-creates autoscaled 0-node pools with the clusterautoscaler-nodetemplate-resources.ate.dev/kvm=4096 label and references them in the spec.priorities[].nodepools field of the ComputeClass. Yes (true 0 nodes, no idle compute cost) Yes, across the pre-created node pools You want true scale-to-zero without maintaining standby capacity buffers.

Example: ComputeClass with the minimumCapacity field

When you use the minimumCapacity field, every entry in the spec.priorities field must specify an explicit machineType field instead of only specifying the machineFamily field:

apiVersion: cloud.google.com/v1
kind: ComputeClass
metadata:
  name: substrate-microvm
spec:
  priorityDefaults:
    enableNestedVirtualization: true
    nodeSystemConfig:
      linuxNodeConfig:
        sysctls:
          fs.inotify.max_user_instances: 65536
          fs.inotify.max_user_watches: 1048576
          net.ipv4.neigh.default.gc_thresh1: 4096
          net.ipv4.neigh.default.gc_thresh2: 16384
          net.ipv4.neigh.default.gc_thresh3: 32768
  priorities:
  - machineType: n4-standard-4
  - machineType: c3-standard-4
  - machineType: n2-standard-4
  nodePoolAutoCreation:
    enabled: true
  minimumCapacity:
    targetNodeCount: 1
  nodePoolConfig:
    imageType: cos_containerd
  whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotScaleUp

To target a WorkerPool to this ComputeClass, add the nodeSelector: {cloud.google.com/compute-class: substrate-microvm} field to the WorkerPool Pod template.

When a ComputeClass falls back across different x86 machine series (such as from N4 to C3 or N2), restoring a durable snapshot at memory fidelity (the SNAPSHOT_FIDELITY_MEMORY mode) requires a Worker whose CPU features are a superset of the snapshot's CPU features. If no compatible Worker has capacity, Agent Substrate downgrades the restore to root-file-system fidelity (the SNAPSHOT_FIDELITY_ROOTFS mode), which preserves root file system and durable volume data while restarting the Actor's processes.

Note: Setting the spec.minimumCapacity.targetNodeCount: 1 field at the ComputeClass level falls back to secondary priorities (the c3-standard-4 or n2-standard-4 machine types) only if the primary priority (the n4-standard-4 machine type) is unavailable when provisioning that first node. After the primary priority provisions one node, the fallback priorities remain at zero nodes and can't scale from zero during mid-burst resource unavailability because pending microVM Worker Pods request the ate.dev/kvm: 1 extended resource. To allow mid-burst fallback across priorities with the minimumCapacity field, set the minimumCapacity.targetNodeCount: 1 field on each fallback entry under the spec.priorities[] field, which keeps one warm node running per priority. Alternatively, use capacity buffers or pre-created 0-node pools.

Example: Scale from zero with pre-created 0-node pools

  1. Save the high-density Linux kernel sysctl settings as a system-config.yaml file:

    linuxConfig:
  sysctl:
    fs.inotify.max_user_instances: '65536'
    fs.inotify.max_user_watches: '1048576'
    net.ipv4.neigh.default.gc_thresh1: '4096'
    net.ipv4.neigh.default.gc_thresh2: '16384'
    net.ipv4.neigh.default.gc_thresh3: '32768'

  2. Pre-create your primary and fallback nested-virtualization node pools at 0 nodes with the --system-config-from-file=system-config.yaml flag and the clusterautoscaler-nodetemplate-resources.ate.dev/kvm=4096 label so the GKE cluster autoscaler knows that the empty pool provides the ate.dev/kvm extended resource:

    # Primary N4 pool (0 nodes)
gcloud container node-pools create microvm-n4-pool \
    --cluster=CLUSTER_NAME \
    --location=LOCATION \
    --machine-type=n4-standard-4 \
    --enable-nested-virtualization \
    --system-config-from-file=system-config.yaml \
    --num-nodes=0 \
    --enable-autoscaling --total-min-nodes=0 --total-max-nodes=10 \
    --node-labels=cloud.google.com/compute-class=substrate-microvm-zero,clusterautoscaler-nodetemplate-resources.ate.dev/kvm=4096 \
    --node-taints=cloud.google.com/compute-class=substrate-microvm-zero:NoSchedule

# Fallback C3 pool (0 nodes)
gcloud container node-pools create microvm-c3-pool \
    --cluster=CLUSTER_NAME \
    --location=LOCATION \
    --machine-type=c3-standard-4 \
    --enable-nested-virtualization \
    --system-config-from-file=system-config.yaml \
    --num-nodes=0 \
    --enable-autoscaling --total-min-nodes=0 --total-max-nodes=10 \
    --node-labels=cloud.google.com/compute-class=substrate-microvm-zero,clusterautoscaler-nodetemplate-resources.ate.dev/kvm=4096 \
    --node-taints=cloud.google.com/compute-class=substrate-microvm-zero:NoSchedule

    Replace the following:

    • CLUSTER_NAME: the name of your GKE Standard cluster.
    • LOCATION: the Compute Engine zone or region of your cluster. Using the --total-min-nodes and --total-max-nodes flags sets the autoscaling bounds across the entire node pool rather than per zone.

  3. Reference the pre-created pools in priority order in your ComputeClass:

    apiVersion: cloud.google.com/v1
kind: ComputeClass
metadata:
  name: substrate-microvm-zero
spec:
  nodePoolAutoCreation:
    enabled: false
  priorities:
  - nodepools:
    - microvm-n4-pool
  - nodepools:
    - microvm-c3-pool
  whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotScaleUp

    The priorityDefaults field doesn't apply to priorities that use the nodepools field, because node settings come from the pre-created node pools. As with auto-created fallback priorities, resuming an Actor on a fallback machine series whose CPU features aren't a superset of the snapshot's CPU features downgrades the restore to the SNAPSHOT_FIDELITY_ROOTFS mode and restarts the Actor's processes.

For more information about ComputeClass configuration, see Control autoscaled node attributes with custom ComputeClasses.

Configure capacity buffers for WorkerPool burst scaling

When an Actor traffic spike exceeds the capacity of your running WorkerPool Pods, new Worker Pods must wait for Compute Engine node provisioning, atelet agent initialization, and sandbox asset prewarming before they can serve Actors. GKE capacity buffers move node provisioning and atelet asset prewarming off the critical path:

  • Active capacity buffers (buffer.x-k8s.io/active-capacity strategy): keep pre-provisioned nodes running and ready so new Worker Pods schedule in one to four seconds, at the full running cost of the Compute Engine VM.
  • Standby capacity buffers (buffer.gke.io/standby-capacity strategy): provision nodes and let the atelet agent initialize and prewarm sandbox assets (the runsc binary or Cloud Hypervisor and Kata images) on disk during the standby initialization window before GKE suspends the Compute Engine VMs. This window defaults to five minutes (5m) and is configured by the buffer.gke.io/standby-capacity-init-time annotation on the CapacityBuffer. Increase the value of this annotation if asset prewarming takes longer than five minutes. When a burst occurs, GKE resumes the suspended nodes in approximately 20 to 35 seconds, and end-to-end WorkerPool readiness (scheduling Worker Pods, issuing Pod certificates, and registering capacity with the ate-api-server component) completes in approximately 50 to 85 seconds. While suspended, you pay only for suspended VM memory and boot disk storage. For example, suspended storage costs approximately 8% of the running compute cost on a c3-standard-4 node with a default 100 GiB hyperdisk-balanced boot disk; the exact percentage varies with machine shape, boot disk size, and provisioned IOPS or throughput.

For more information about buffer strategies, see Strategies to reduce startup latency.

Limitations and rules for capacity buffers

When you configure capacity buffers for Agent Substrate on GKE, apply the following rules:

  • Compute Engine machine-shape restrictions for standby buffers: Compute Engine instance suspension isn't supported on VMs with attached Local SSDs or on machine shapes with more than 208 GB of memory (such as the c3-highmem-88 machine type or bare metal shapes). For large worker node shapes or nodes with Local SSDs, use active capacity buffers instead of standby buffers.
  • Avoid pointing the scalableRef field at a 0-replica WorkerPool or microVM Deployment:
    • The GKE CapacityBuffer controller can't resolve a custom resource (kind: WorkerPool) when the pool is scaled to 0 replicas.
    • For microVM WorkerPool resources, also don't point the scalableRef field at the underlying Deployment, because the Deployment Pod template includes the ate.dev/kvm: 1 extended resource (which prevents node auto-provisioning from scaling out an empty pool). Instead, configure buffers by referencing a PodTemplate (in the podTemplateRef field) that selects the ComputeClass without requesting the ate.dev/kvm extended resource.
    • For gVisor WorkerPool resources (which don't request the ate.dev/kvm extended resource), you can point the scalableRef field directly to the WorkerPool underlying Deployment or use a PodTemplate.

Example: Standby CapacityBuffer using a PodTemplate

The following manifest defines a PodTemplate and a standby CapacityBuffer that work for either microVM or gVisor WorkerPool resources:

apiVersion: v1
kind: PodTemplate
metadata:
  name: substrate-worker-buffer-template
  namespace: WORKERPOOL_NAMESPACE
template:
  spec:
    nodeSelector:
      cloud.google.com/compute-class: COMPUTE_CLASS_NAME
    containers:
    - name: buffer-placeholder
      image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.9
      resources:
        requests:
          cpu: "WORKER_CPU_REQUEST"
          memory: "WORKER_MEMORY_REQUEST"
---
apiVersion: autoscaling.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: CapacityBuffer
metadata:
  name: substrate-standby-buffer
  namespace: WORKERPOOL_NAMESPACE
spec:
  podTemplateRef:
    name: substrate-worker-buffer-template
  replicas: BUFFER_REPLICAS
  provisioningStrategy: buffer.gke.io/standby-capacity

Replace the following:

  • WORKERPOOL_NAMESPACE: the Kubernetes namespace of your WorkerPool (for example, my-workerpool).
  • COMPUTE_CLASS_NAME: the name of the custom ComputeClass targeted by your WorkerPool (for example, substrate-microvm).
  • WORKER_CPU_REQUEST and WORKER_MEMORY_REQUEST: the CPU and memory requests of a single Worker Pod in your WorkerPool (for example, 2 CPUs and 4Gi of memory on a 4-vCPU node), leaving node capacity for the atelet agent and GKE system daemons. Matching these values to one Worker Pod's requests helps ensure that each buffer replica provisions one standby worker node rather than packing multiple buffer placeholders onto a single node.
  • BUFFER_REPLICAS: the number of standby worker nodes to keep prewarmed (for example, 4 nodes).

When you use standby capacity buffers, add a toleration for the buffer.gke.io/standby-capacity-node-suspended taint (with the operator: "Exists" field) to the atelet DaemonSet so that replacement atelet Pods can remain scheduled on suspended standby nodes (for example, during a DaemonSet rolling update). For an example DaemonSet configuration, see Preload images on standby buffers.

If multiple workloads share the same ComputeClass, add matching workload-separation tolerations and nodeSelector labels to both your WorkerPool Pod template and the buffer PodTemplate so that GKE provisions dedicated tainted nodes that other workloads don't claim. Also add a matching toleration to the atelet DaemonSet so that the atelet agent can schedule on those dedicated nodes. For step-by-step instructions, see Configure capacity buffers.

Manage upgrades and autoscaler interactions

This section describes how to manage atelet DaemonSet updates, cluster autoscaler scale-down events, and node upgrades without disrupting active Actors.

Update the atelet DaemonSet with standby buffers

Suspended standby buffer nodes carry the buffer.gke.io/standby-capacity-node-suspended taint and an unreachable taint while suspended, so the kubelet agent on a suspended node can't acknowledge Pod deletions. Ensure that the atelet DaemonSet tolerates the buffer.gke.io/standby-capacity-node-suspended taint (with the operator: "Exists" field). Even with that toleration, during a standard rolling update of the atelet DaemonSet (with the maxUnavailable: 1 field), Pods on suspended nodes enter the Terminating state and can block the update from progressing on running nodes.

Before you update the atelet DaemonSet on a cluster with suspended standby nodes, do one of the following:

  • So unreachable standby nodes don't exhaust the update budget, set the spec.updateStrategy.rollingUpdate.maxUnavailable field on the atelet DaemonSet to a value greater than the maximum number of suspended standby nodes.

  • Before you update the atelet DaemonSet, temporarily scale your standby CapacityBuffer replicas to 0 and wait until the cluster autoscaler removes all suspended standby buffer nodes (typically 10 to 15 minutes). To check whether any nodes still report a Suspended condition status of True, run the following command:

    kubectl get nodes -o custom-columns='NAME:.metadata.name,SUSPENDED:.status.conditions[?(@.type=="Suspended")].status'

Protect active Actors during scale-down and upgrades

Because active Actors execute inside sandboxes managed by the atelet agent rather than as individual Kubernetes Pods, a node's CPU and memory requests might appear low to the GKE cluster autoscaler even while a Worker Pod on that node is hosting active Actors. When a node is drained, the kubelet agent sends a SIGTERM signal to the Worker Pod, and the Worker forwards the SIGTERM signal to the main process of each container of every Actor that it hosts. Each active Actor then has up to 30 minutes to be suspended before the Worker stops. Give every stateful Actor a SIGTERM handler that doesn't exit on the signal and that calls the SuspendActor method with the DURABILITY_MODE_SYNCHRONOUS mode. An Actor whose main process exits on the SIGTERM signal loses unsaved state immediately. If the Worker Pod stops while still hosting an active Actor, then the Actor enters the ACTOR_STATE_CRASHED state.

To minimize disruptions during scale-down events and GKE cluster upgrades, apply the following practices:

  • Avoid using Spot VMs for stateful WorkerPool nodes, because Spot VM preemption provides only 15 seconds to 2 minutes of termination notice before stopping the node.
  • Coordinate draining in your orchestrator so active Actors are checkpointed and suspended before Worker Pods stop, or prevent the cluster autoscaler from evicting active Worker Pods (for example, by using the cluster-autoscaler.kubernetes.io/safe-to-evict: "false" Pod annotation). If you set the safe-to-evict: "false" annotation statically in the WorkerPool Pod template, then the cluster autoscaler won't scale down a node while a Worker Pod is scheduled on it—even when that Worker hosts zero active Actors. To release idle nodes, you must scale down WorkerPool replicas or manage the annotation dynamically. For more information about the Worker eviction lifecycle and recovering crashed Actors with the RevertActor method, see Eviction in the Agent Substrate API guide.
  • Configure GKE surge upgrades and review Upgrade in a resource-constrained environment so new worker nodes are provisioned before existing worker nodes are cordoned and drained.

What's next

  • Learn how to choose the right orchestration model, sandbox runtime, isolation controls, and storage options in Plan an architecture for AI agent workloads on GKE.
  • Learn more about GKE custom ComputeClasses and GKE capacity buffers.
  • Explore more resources in the Agent Substrate GitHub repository.

Choose storage for AI agentic workloads

This document helps you select an appropriate storage option for your AI agents based on their specific data lifecycle needs and latency requirements.

For implementation details, see Manage Agent Sandbox on GKE storage.

Considerations for choosing a storage solution

When choosing a storage solution for your AI agents, you should consider your agentic platform requirements, such as performance and scale, and your agents' data management requirements.

Platform requirements

Evaluate the following operational and architectural requirements of your platform:

  • Platform scale and agents churn frequency (control plane): the number of concurrent agents, and the number of agents created, paused, reactivated, and deleted per minute. Platforms creating thousands of agents per minute or pausing idle agents require storage with low-latency attach and mount operations at significant scale (for example, Filestore mounts faster than Hyperdisk can attach).
  • Dataset size and load latency (data plane): agents loading multi-gigabyte datasets or heavy libraries (such as Node.js or Python packages) during startup require high storage I/O performance for reading the data in seconds (for example, Hyperdisk offers high per-disk read throughput).
  • Agent cold-start and reactivation latency: the expected latency, such as sub-second or multi-second. Achieving sub-second startup latency requires using Agent Sandbox on GKE Warm Pools. Using direct sandbox creation generally incurs a multi-second delay for Pod startup and dynamic disk attachment.
  • Storage size per agent: depending on the service chosen, you must accommodate provisioning limits, such as a minimum size of 4 GiB for Google Cloud Hyperdisk or a minimum of 10 GiB for a single Filestore share.
  • Data access modes and isolation: how the platform should support workspace isolation and collaborative workspaces. This determines whether your agents will need private isolated workspaces (ReadWriteOnce), collaborative workspaces (ReadWriteMany), or exploration branching workspaces (Read-Only template with a writable scratchpad).
  • Resilience: if your agents specifically require regional resilience, Filestore Multishares for GKE (Enterprise) is the appropriate choice.
  • Storage cost: storage services vary significantly in price, with Hyperdisk Balanced offering a cost-efficient option compared to Filestore Multishares.

Agent data lifecycle patterns

When you decide how your solution handles persistent and ephemeral data, consider the following agent data lifecycle patterns:

  • Stateful workspace (continuous state): the workspace maintains a continuous state across sessions. The agent preserves its data when it is paused (the Agent Sandbox is deleted) and restores that data from the latest saved state when reactivated (the Sandbox is re-created).
  • Point-in-time restore and ownership transfer (snapshot state): the workspace acts as a snapshot state, meaning it branches off from a frozen point in time. The workspace is initialized from a historical dataset or another user's shared state, to execute an ownership transfer. Subsequent modifications are saved to a separate, private writable layer, leaving the master copy untouched. This pattern is useful for scenarios like cloning a dataset to run parallel experiments, debugging, or performing independent work based on shared data.
  • Ephemeral workspace (scratch state): the workspace provides a temporary scratch state where no data is preserved. The agent uses a storage volume strictly for holding temporary files while it is active. When the agent is paused or deleted (Agent Sandbox deletion), the temporary data is permanently discarded.

Agent data access modes

Choose a storage service that supports your agents' needs if they need to access storage in one of these data access modes:

  • Private isolated workspace: an agent starts up with a private isolated storage directory it has sole read and write access to.
  • Collaborative workspace: multiple coordinating agents mount the exact same shared directory in Read-Write (RW) mode to collaboratively update files in real time.
  • Exploration branching workspace: the agent accesses base template files in Read-Only (RO) mode to avoid altering the template, and makes new writes either by routing them to a separate local emptyDir scratchpad or private persistent path or by copying the template files directly into a private writable workspace on startup.

Compare storage options for Agent Sandbox on GKE

Consider the following scenarios to help you compare your storage options:

  • Use Hyperdisk Balanced for cost-efficient storage for agents that tolerate a few seconds startup latency and use a private isolated workspace with ReadWriteOnce (RWO) access mode.
  • Use Filestore Multishares for GKE (Enterprise) for agents that require a collaborative workspace or regional resilience.
Note: Filestore Multishares for Agent Storage is available in Preview. This service improves performance and lowers costs per agent compared to Filestore Multishares for GKE (Enterprise). It offers faster provisioning latency, more shares per instance, and smaller share sizes. To try this Preview release, contact your account team.

Manage Agent Sandbox on GKE storage

This document provides reference implementations for managing storage for Agent Sandbox on GKE tailored to your agents' data lifecycle needs.

Depending on your agents' data lifecycle needs, choose one of the following configurations:

  • Configure a stateful workspace
  • Configure a point-in-time restore and ownership transfer
  • Configure an ephemeral workspace

For more information about choosing a storage solution, see Choose storage for AI agentic workloads.

The following document uses the dynamic-rwo StorageClass for automated disk type selection to provision disks compatible with machine types of nodes where Agent Sandbox on GKE Pods are scheduled. To help ensure that GKE provisions Hyperdisk Balanced volumes for your agents' storage, you must schedule your Agent Sandbox on GKE Pods on the nodes of compatible machine families, such as N4; otherwise, GKE falls back to pd-balanced.

This document implements the Private Isolated Workspace data access mode by using ReadWriteOnce (RWO) access. In this mode, an agent starts up with a private isolated storage directory it has sole read and write access to.

Unless otherwise specified, the reference implementations in this document use direct sandbox creation, which is applicable to agents that tolerate multi-second startup latency. To achieve sub-second startup latency for stateful or point-in-time restore workspaces, you must use Agent Sandbox on GKE Warm Pools. Binding storage to a claimed Warm Pool Pod requires custom scripting and a privileged DaemonSet. For a reference implementation, see this GitHub example.

Alternative access modes

To support alternative access modes, you can modify the volume and snapshot definitions in the configurations:

  • Collaborative workspace: change the accessModes to ReadWriteMany and use an RWX-capable StorageClass, such as Filestore Multishares (Enterprise) (enterprise-multishare-rwx).
  • Exploration branching workspace: mount the template folder as read-only and providing a separate writable scratchpad. For the base template, you must use storage supporting multiple read-only attachments, such as Hyperdisk ML with ReadOnlyMany (ROX) access mode or Filestore Multishares with RWX access mode.

Before you begin

Make sure that you have a GKE cluster that has the Agent Sandbox controller installed. If you don't, complete only the following sections of Install Agent Sandbox on GKE, and then return to this document:

  1. Define environment variables
  2. Create a GKE cluster
  3. Install Agent Sandbox
  4. Apply the recommended security policy

If you completed the Deploy a sandboxed environment section of that document, delete the sample resources that it created so that your nodes have enough capacity for the sandboxes in this document:

kubectl delete sandboxclaim sandbox-claim --ignore-not-found
kubectl delete sandboxwarmpool python-runtime-warmpool --ignore-not-found
kubectl delete sandbox sandbox-example-2 --ignore-not-found

Configure a stateful workspace

Use this pattern to preserve the latest state of an agent's files. It is useful when your agent must preserve the state when the agent session is paused or terminated (Agent Sandbox is deleted) and restore the data from the latest state when the agent session is activated (Agent Sandbox is re-created).

The reference implementation in this section uses direct sandbox creation and is applicable to agents that tolerate multi-second startup latency.

This approach uses standard GKE PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) resources to link a sandbox to a pre-existing PVC containing a user's data.

The stateful workspace pattern follows this sequence of events:

  1. Provisioning: the administrator or orchestrator manually provisions a private PVC for each agent session using a deterministic identifier (for example, pvc-agent-1).
  2. Referencing: in the Sandbox resource, you use the persistentVolumeClaim field within the volumes block to specify the exact claimName of the existing volume.
  3. Latency: when the sandbox is created, GKE must dynamically attach the Compute Engine disk to the node VM, which incurs a standard multi-second delay.
  4. Persistence: on session termination (deleting the Sandbox resource), GKE detaches the disk but does not destroy the PVC, which helps to ensure that the latest state is preserved for the next session.

To configure a stateful workspace that preserves data between sessions, complete the steps in the following subsections.

Provision a persistent workspace (PVC)

Create a private PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) that uses a deterministic identifier, such as pvc-agent-1.

  1. Save the following manifest as pvc-agent-1.yaml:

    apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: pvc-agent-1 # Derived directly from the deterministic assignment ID
  namespace: default
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  storageClassName: dynamic-rwo # Selects disk type compatible with the node machine family
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 10Gi

  2. Apply the manifest:

    kubectl apply -f pvc-agent-1.yaml

Because the storage class uses dynamic volume binding, the disk is not attached to any node yet. It remains in a Pending state until a Pod requesting it is scheduled.

Deploy the Agent Sandbox

Deploy the Sandbox custom resource, referencing the deterministic PVC.

  1. Save the following manifest as sandbox-agent-1.yaml:

    apiVersion: agents.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Sandbox
metadata:
  name: sandbox-agent-1 # Traceable sandbox name
  namespace: default
spec:
  podTemplate:
    spec:
      runtimeClassName: gvisor # Required
      automountServiceAccountToken: false # Required
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true # Required
        runAsUser: 1000
        fsGroup: 1000 # Grant group access to the volume
      nodeSelector:
        sandbox.gke.io/runtime: gvisor # Required
      tolerations:
      - key: "sandbox.gke.io/runtime"
        value: "gvisor"
        effect: "NoSchedule" # Required
      containers:
      - name: agent
        image: registry.k8s.io/agent-sandbox/python-runtime-sandbox:v0.1.0
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8888
        volumeMounts:
        - name: workspace-disk
          mountPath: /workspace # Mounts the private disk into the container
        resources:
          limits:
            cpu: "500m"
            memory: "1Gi" # Required
        securityContext:
          capabilities:
            drop: ["ALL"] # Required
      volumes:
      - name: workspace-disk
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: pvc-agent-1 # Binds this specific Sandbox to Agent 1's PVC
      restartPolicy: OnFailure

  2. Apply the manifest:

    kubectl apply -f sandbox-agent-1.yaml

  3. Wait until the sandbox is ready:

    kubectl wait sandbox sandbox-agent-1 \
    --for=condition=Ready \
    --timeout=300s

    GKE verifies node capacity and attaches the disk, which takes a few seconds. The container initializes inside a userspace gVisor kernel. In an Autopilot cluster, the sandbox can take several minutes to become ready because GKE might need to create a node for it.

Write data from the agent

Simulate an active AI agent executing file modifications inside its workspace by writing a text file to the mounted disk.

# Set the active Pod name
POD_NAME=sandbox-agent-1

# Write a state file to the persistent directory
kubectl exec ${POD_NAME} -- sh -c "echo 'Workspace State Saved - Agent 1' > /workspace/modified_data.txt"

# Confirm the file exists on the disk
kubectl exec ${POD_NAME} -- cat /workspace/modified_data.txt

End the agent session

To simulate scaling down or terminating the session when the agent goes idle, delete the Sandbox resource but preserve the underlying storage.

kubectl delete sandbox sandbox-agent-1

GKE unmounts and detaches the disk. The pvc-agent-1 PVC remains, preserving the data.

Reactivate the agent session

To reactivate the session, redeploy a fresh Sandbox resource that references the same PVC, and then wait until the sandbox is ready:

kubectl apply -f sandbox-agent-1.yaml

kubectl wait sandbox sandbox-agent-1 \
    --for=condition=Ready \
    --timeout=300s

The disk is re-attached (incurring the attachment delay), and the container boots up.

Verify data preservation

Inspect the newly created sandbox container to verify that the previous session data was preserved.

# Set the active Pod name of the new session
NEW_POD_NAME=sandbox-agent-1

# Read the file from the newly booted sandbox
kubectl exec ${NEW_POD_NAME} -- cat /workspace/modified_data.txt

The output should show Workspace State Saved - Agent 1.

Clean up resources

Delete the Agent Sandbox and the associated persistent volume claim:

kubectl delete sandbox sandbox-agent-1
kubectl delete pvc pvc-agent-1

Configure a point-in-time restore and ownership transfer

Use this pattern to clone datasets for running parallel experiments, debugging, or independent work. An agent's workspace is initialized from a historical dataset (or shared state), saving subsequent modifications to a separate, private writable layer without modifying the base template.

The reference implementation in this section uses direct sandbox creation and is applicable to agents that tolerate multi-second startup latency. This approach relies on the orchestrator to dynamically provision new PersistentVolumeClaims (PVCs) from historical VolumeSnapshots before launching a fresh sandbox session.

Create the VolumeSnapshotClass

Create a VolumeSnapshotClass that specifies the CSI driver and deletion policy. For Hyperdisk, use the pd.csi.storage.gke.io driver.

  1. Save the following manifest as 1-snapshot-class.yaml:

    apiVersion: snapshot.storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: VolumeSnapshotClass
metadata:
  name: standard-rwo-snapshot
driver: pd.csi.storage.gke.io
deletionPolicy: Delete

  2. Apply the manifest:

    kubectl apply -f 1-snapshot-class.yaml

Provision the initial workspace

Create a volume where the agent will perform its initial work.

  1. Save the following manifest as 2-source-pvc.yaml:

    apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: agent-source-pvc
spec:
  accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
  storageClassName: dynamic-rwo
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 10Gi

  2. Apply the manifest:

    kubectl apply -f 2-source-pvc.yaml

Generate state data

Deploy a sandbox Pod to write data to the volume.

  1. Save the following manifest as 3-source-sandbox.yaml:

    apiVersion: agents.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Sandbox
metadata:
  name: agent-session-v1
  namespace: default
spec:
  podTemplate:
    spec:
      runtimeClassName: gvisor
      automountServiceAccountToken: false # Required
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true # Required
        runAsUser: 1000
        fsGroup: 1000 # Grant group access to the volume
      nodeSelector:
        sandbox.gke.io/runtime: gvisor # Required
      tolerations:
      - key: "sandbox.gke.io/runtime"
        value: "gvisor"
        effect: "NoSchedule" # Required
      containers:
      - name: agent
        image: registry.k8s.io/agent-sandbox/python-runtime-sandbox:v0.1.0
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8888
        volumeMounts:
        - name: workspace
          mountPath: /workspace
        resources:
          limits:
            cpu: "500m"
            memory: "1Gi" # Required
        securityContext:
          capabilities:
            drop: ["ALL"] # Required
      volumes:
      - name: workspace
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: agent-source-pvc
      restartPolicy: OnFailure

  2. Apply the manifest:

    kubectl apply -f 3-source-sandbox.yaml

  3. Wait until the sandbox is ready, and then write a state file. The sync command flushes the write to disk so that the snapshot in the next section includes the file's contents:

    kubectl wait sandbox agent-session-v1 \
    --for=condition=Ready \
    --timeout=300s

POD_NAME=agent-session-v1
kubectl exec ${POD_NAME} -- sh -c "echo 'Point-in-Time Snapshot - v1' > /workspace/state.txt && sync"

Archive the historical state (CSI VolumeSnapshot)

Trigger a CSI VolumeSnapshot to freeze the current state. When taking a snapshot, follow the best practices for disk snapshots.

  1. Save the following manifest as 4-volume-snapshot.yaml:

    apiVersion: snapshot.storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: VolumeSnapshot
metadata:
  name: agent-session-v1-snapshot
spec:
  volumeSnapshotClassName: standard-rwo-snapshot
  source:
    persistentVolumeClaimName: agent-source-pvc

  2. Apply the manifest:

    kubectl apply -f 4-volume-snapshot.yaml

  3. Wait until the snapshot is ready to use:

    kubectl wait volumesnapshot agent-session-v1-snapshot \
    --for=jsonpath='{.status.readyToUse}'=true \
    --timeout=600s

Restore the volume from the snapshot

Deploy a new PVC with its dataSource pointing to the CSI VolumeSnapshot.

  1. Save the following manifest as 5-restored-pvc.yaml:

    apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: agent-restored-pvc
spec:
  accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
  storageClassName: dynamic-rwo
  dataSource:
    name: agent-session-v1-snapshot
    kind: VolumeSnapshot
    apiGroup: snapshot.storage.k8s.io
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 10Gi

  2. Apply the manifest:

    kubectl apply -f 5-restored-pvc.yaml

Launch the restored Agent Sandbox session

Provision a fresh Sandbox resource that references the newly restored PVC.

  1. Save the following manifest as 6-restored-sandbox.yaml:

    apiVersion: agents.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Sandbox
metadata:
  name: agent-session-v2-restored
  namespace: default
spec:
  podTemplate:
    spec:
      runtimeClassName: gvisor
      automountServiceAccountToken: false # Required
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true # Required
        runAsUser: 1000
        fsGroup: 1000 # Grant group access to the volume
      nodeSelector:
        sandbox.gke.io/runtime: gvisor # Required
      tolerations:
      - key: "sandbox.gke.io/runtime"
        value: "gvisor"
        effect: "NoSchedule" # Required
      containers:
      - name: agent
        image: registry.k8s.io/agent-sandbox/python-runtime-sandbox:v0.1.0
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8888
        volumeMounts:
        - name: workspace
          mountPath: /workspace
        resources:
          limits:
            cpu: "500m"
            memory: "1Gi" # Required
        securityContext:
          capabilities:
            drop: ["ALL"] # Required
      volumes:
      - name: workspace
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: agent-restored-pvc
      restartPolicy: OnFailure

  2. Apply the manifest:

    kubectl apply -f 6-restored-sandbox.yaml

  3. Wait until the sandbox is ready:

    kubectl wait sandbox agent-session-v2-restored \
    --for=condition=Ready \
    --timeout=600s

    This sandbox can take longer to become ready than the source sandbox because GKE creates its disk from the snapshot after the snapshot is ready.

Verify persistence and restoration

Verify that the agent can read the historical data.

NEW_POD_NAME=agent-session-v2-restored
kubectl exec ${NEW_POD_NAME} -- cat /workspace/state.txt

Expected Output: Point-in-Time Snapshot - v1

Clean up resources

Delete the Agent Sandboxes, PVCs, and the VolumeSnapshot:

kubectl delete sandbox agent-session-v1
kubectl delete sandbox agent-session-v2-restored
kubectl delete pvc agent-source-pvc
kubectl delete pvc agent-restored-pvc
kubectl delete volumesnapshot agent-session-v1-snapshot
kubectl delete volumesnapshotclass standard-rwo-snapshot

Configure an ephemeral workspace

Use the ephemeral workspace pattern when an agent needs a storage volume for storing temporary files while the agent is active. No data needs to be preserved on Agent Sandbox deletion.

Configure with sub-second startup

Use Agent Sandbox on GKE Warm Pools to pre-provision empty volumes in the background.

Define the SandboxTemplate resource

Define the ephemeral storage backing within the volumeClaimTemplate block.

  1. Save the following manifest as stateless-template.yaml:

    apiVersion: extensions.agents.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: SandboxTemplate
metadata:
  name: stateless-sandbox-template
  namespace: default
spec:
  podTemplate:
    spec:
      runtimeClassName: gvisor
      automountServiceAccountToken: false
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
        runAsUser: 1000
        fsGroup: 1000 # Grant group access to the volume
      nodeSelector:
        sandbox.gke.io/runtime: gvisor
      tolerations:
      - key: "sandbox.gke.io/runtime"
        value: "gvisor"
        effect: "NoSchedule"
      containers:
      - name: agent
        image: registry.k8s.io/agent-sandbox/python-runtime-sandbox:v0.1.0
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8888
        volumeMounts:
        - name: ephemeral-disk
          mountPath: /workspace
        resources:
          limits:
            cpu: "500m"
            memory: "1Gi" # Required
        securityContext:
          capabilities:
            drop: ["ALL"] # Required
  volumeClaimTemplates:
  - metadata:
      name: ephemeral-disk
    spec:
      accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
      storageClassName: dynamic-rwo # Selects disk type compatible with node machine family
      resources:
        requests:
          storage: 10Gi

Launch the SandboxWarmPool resource

  1. Save the following manifest as stateless-warmpool.yaml:

    apiVersion: extensions.agents.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: SandboxWarmPool
metadata:
  name: stateless-warmpool
  namespace: default
spec:
  replicas: 2 # Keep two standby Pods with pre-attached empty disks
  sandboxTemplateRef:
    name: stateless-sandbox-template

  2. Apply both manifests:

    kubectl apply -f stateless-template.yaml
kubectl apply -f stateless-warmpool.yaml

  3. Wait until the warm pool's sandboxes are ready:

    kubectl wait sandboxwarmpool stateless-warmpool \
    --for=jsonpath='{.status.readyReplicas}'=2 \
    --timeout=600s

    If you create a SandboxClaim resource before the pool's sandboxes are ready, the controller might create a new sandbox for the claim instead of assigning one from the pool. In an Autopilot cluster, the sandboxes can take several minutes to become ready because GKE might need to create nodes for them.

Create a SandboxClaim resource

Define a SandboxClaim resource that triggers when a user starts a session.

  1. Save the following manifest as stateless-sandbox-claim.yaml:

    apiVersion: extensions.agents.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: SandboxClaim
metadata:
  name: agent-1-claim
spec:
  warmPoolRef:
    name: stateless-warmpool

  2. Apply the manifest:

    kubectl apply -f stateless-sandbox-claim.yaml

Verify sub-second execution

Wait until the claim is ready, capture the Agent Sandbox Pod name, and then verify that the /workspace directory is mounted and ready for immediate use:

kubectl wait sandboxclaim agent-1-claim --for=condition=Ready --timeout=300s
export POD_NAME=$(kubectl get sandboxclaim agent-1-claim -o jsonpath='{.status.sandbox.name}')
kubectl exec ${POD_NAME} -- ls -la /workspace

Terminate the agent session

To end the agent session, delete the SandboxClaim resource. Deleting the claim also deletes the claimed sandbox and its volume:

kubectl delete sandboxclaim agent-1-claim

Clean up resources

Delete the SandboxWarmPool and SandboxTemplate resources:

kubectl delete sandboxwarmpool stateless-warmpool
kubectl delete sandboxtemplate stateless-sandbox-template

Configure with multi-second startup

To implement an ephemeral workspace that tolerates multi-second latency, use direct Agent Sandbox creation without a Warm Pool.

Define a stateless Agent Sandbox

  1. Save the following manifest as sandbox-direct-stateless.yaml:

    apiVersion: agents.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Sandbox
metadata:
  name: sandbox-direct-stateless
  namespace: default
spec:
  podTemplate:
    spec:
      runtimeClassName: gvisor
      automountServiceAccountToken: false
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
        runAsUser: 1000
        fsGroup: 1000 # Grant group access to the volume
      nodeSelector:
        sandbox.gke.io/runtime: gvisor
      tolerations:
      - key: "sandbox.gke.io/runtime"
        value: "gvisor"
        effect: "NoSchedule"
      containers:
      - name: agent
        image: registry.k8s.io/agent-sandbox/python-runtime-sandbox:v0.1.0
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8888
        volumeMounts:
        - name: ephemeral-disk
          mountPath: /workspace
        resources:
          limits:
            cpu: "500m"
            memory: "1Gi" # Required
        securityContext:
          capabilities:
            drop: ["ALL"] # Required
      restartPolicy: OnFailure
  volumeClaimTemplates:
  - metadata:
      name: ephemeral-disk
    spec:
      accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
      storageClassName: dynamic-rwo
      resources:
        requests:
          storage: 10Gi

Deploy the Agent Sandbox

To dynamically provision the disk and attach it to the scheduled node, apply the manifest:

kubectl apply -f sandbox-direct-stateless.yaml

Verify startup latency and execution

Monitor the Pod status to observe the attachment delay before the Pod transitions to the Running state:

kubectl get pods -w

When the Pod is running, press Control+C to stop watching.

Capture the Pod name and verify that the /workspace directory is available:

POD_NAME=sandbox-direct-stateless
kubectl exec ${POD_NAME} -- ls -la /workspace

Terminate agent session

Delete the Sandbox resource to automatically terminate the Pod and destroy its ephemeral storage:

kubectl delete sandbox sandbox-direct-stateless

What's next

  • Learn more about Agent Sandbox on GKE.
  • Learn more about isolating AI code execution with Agent Sandbox on GKE.
  • Learn how to Save and restore Agent Sandbox on GKE environments with Pod snapshots.

tutorials/agentic-adk-vllm:
Deploy an agentic AI application on GKE with the Agent Development Kit (ADK) and a self-hosted LLM

Note: This tutorial demonstrates a legacy approach that executes agentic AI application code in standard, un-isolated Pods. To isolate untrusted code from your host kernel and internal, refer to our Deploying Secure AI Agents on GKE, Code Generation Agent on GKE, and High-Performance Distributed Reinforcement Learning on GKE codelabs instead.

This tutorial demonstrates how to deploy and manage containerized agentic AI/ML applications by using Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). By combining the Google Agent Development Kit (ADK) with a self-hosted large language model (LLM) like Llama 3.1 served by vLLM, you can operationalize AI agents efficiently and at scale while maintaining full control over the model stack. This tutorial walks you through the end-to-end process of taking a Python-based agent from development to production deployment on a GKE Autopilot cluster with GPU acceleration.

This tutorial is intended for Machine learning (ML) engineers, Developers, and Cloud architects who are interested in using Kubernetes container orchestration capabilities for serving agentic AI/ML applications. To learn more about common roles and example tasks that we reference in Google Cloud content, see Common GKE user roles and tasks.

Note: The approach in this tutorial requires provisioning a GKE cluster with GPU hardware to run the LLM, which is different from the Vertex AI approach, where model inference is handled by Google's managed infrastructure. For more information about the Vertex AI approach, see Deploy an agentic AI application on GKE with the ADK and Vertex AI.

Before you begin, ensure you are familiar with the following:

  • GKE
  • Containerization with Docker

Background

This section describes the key technologies used in this tutorial.

Agent Development Kit (ADK)

Agent Development Kit (ADK) is a flexible and modular framework for developing and deploying AI agents. Although it's optimized for Gemini and the Google ecosystem, ADK doesn't require you to use a specific model or deployment, and is built for compatibility with other frameworks. ADK was designed to make agent development feel more like software development, to make it easier for developers to create, deploy, and orchestrate agentic architectures that range from basic tasks to complex workflows.

For more information, see the ADK documentation.

GKE managed Kubernetes service

Google Cloud offers a range of services, including GKE, which is well-suited to deploying and managing AI/ML workloads. GKE is a managed Kubernetes service that simplifies deploying, scaling, and managing containerized applications. GKE provides the necessary infrastructure—including scalable resources, distributed computing, and efficient networking—to handle the computational demands of LLMs.

For more information about key Kubernetes concepts, see Start learning about Kubernetes. For more information about the GKE and how it helps you scale, automate, and manage Kubernetes, see GKE overview.

vLLM

vLLM is a highly optimized open source LLM serving framework that can increase serving throughput on GPUs, with features such as the following:

  • Optimized transformer implementation with PagedAttention.
  • Continuous batching to improve the overall serving throughput.
  • Tensor parallelism and distributed serving on multiple GPUs.

For more information, see the vLLM documentation.

Objectives

This tutorial shows you how to do the following:

  1. Set up your Google Cloud environment.
  2. Provision a GPU-enabled GKE cluster.
  3. Deploy a Llama 3.1 model by using the vLLM inference server.
  4. Build a container image for your ADK-based agent.
  5. Deploy the agent to the GKE cluster and connect it to the self-hosted LLM.
  6. Test your deployed agent.

Architecture

This tutorial presents a scalable architecture for deploying agentic AI applications on GKE. The ADK agent application runs on a standard CPU node pool and the self-hosted LLM (Llama 3.1 on vLLM) runs on a GPU-enabled node pool, both within the same GKE cluster. This architecture separates the agent's application logic from the LLM inference workload, which allows each component to be scaled and managed independently.

The architecture has two core components, each on its own GKE Deployment:

  • ADK agent application: your agent's custom-built business logic and tools (like get_weather) are in a container image. The image runs on a standard CPU node pool and communicates with the LLM using an internal Kubernetes service.

  • Self-hosted LLM (Llama 3.1 on vLLM): the Llama 3.1 model runs on a dedicated vLLM server on a GPU-enabled node pool. This deployment uses a public container image (vllm/vllm-openai:v0.8.5) that's configured to download and serve the specified model from Hugging Face when the container starts. The agent communicates with this server through a REST API exposed by the vllm-llama3-service Kubernetes service.

Both the ADK agent and the vLLM deployments run on the same GKE cluster. This colocation within a single cluster simplifies networking, management, and deployment while still allowing for specialized hardware assignment for components of the application.

Costs

This tutorial uses the following billable components of Google Cloud:

  • GKE
  • Artifact Registry
  • Cloud Build

Review the pricing for each service to understand potential costs.

Before you begin

  • Sign in to your Google Cloud account. If you're new to Google Cloud, create an account to evaluate how our products perform in real-world scenarios. New customers also get $300 in free credits to run, test, and deploy workloads.

  • In the Google Cloud console, on the project selector page, select or create a Google Cloud project.

    Roles required to select or create a project

    • Select a project: Selecting a project doesn't require a specific IAM role—you can select any project that you've been granted a role on.
    • Create a project: To create a project, you need the Project Creator role (roles/resourcemanager.projectCreator), which contains the resourcemanager.projects.create permission. Learn how to grant roles.
    Note: If you don't plan to keep the resources that you create in this procedure, create a project instead of selecting an existing project. After you finish these steps, you can delete the project, removing all resources associated with the project.

Otherwise, you can get this permission through the Service Usage Admin role (roles/serviceusage.serviceUsageAdmin). Learn how to grant roles.
