About multi-cluster Gateways

This document describes how multi-cluster Gateways operate within Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). Multi-cluster Gateways are a powerful networking solution that let you manage traffic for services deployed across multiple GKE clusters.

This document is for Cloud architects and Networking specialists who design and architect their organization's network. To learn more about common roles and example tasks that we reference in Google Cloud content, see Common GKE Enterprise user roles and tasks.

Overview

Multi-cluster Gateway is configured by using the Kubernetes Gateway API resources. The GKE Gateway controller watches these resources (Gateway, HTTPRoute) and automatically provisions and maintains the required Google Cloud global load-balancing infrastructure. This infrastructure provides advanced traffic management for services deployed across multiple GKE clusters within a fleet. Multi-cluster Gateways uses Google Cloud's global load-balancing infrastructure to provide a single, unified entry point for your applications. This approach has the following benefits:

  • Simplifies management
  • Improves reliability
  • Enables advanced traffic management capabilities

Traffic management capabilities

Multi-cluster Gateways provide you with advanced capabilities to manage traffic across multiple clusters. You can implement sophisticated routing strategies, such as phased rollouts and blue-green strategies, to safely deploy changes. For fine-grained control, you can use header-based matching to test changes with a small percentage of traffic, or split traffic by weight to gradually shift requests between different cluster backends.

Multi-cluster Gateways also let you mirror traffic, which sends a copy of live user requests to a new service to test performance without impacting users. To ensure reliability and prevent overloads, multi-cluster Gateways support health-based failover and capacity-based load balancing, which distributes requests based on the defined capacity of your services.

How multi-cluster Gateway works

All GKE clusters that participate in a multi-cluster Gateway setup must be registered to a fleet. A fleet provides a logical grouping of clusters, which enables consistent management and communication across the clusters. One GKE cluster within the fleet is designated as the config cluster.

The config cluster acts as a centralized control point for your multi-cluster Gateway configuration. You deploy all multi-cluster Gateway API resources, such as Gateway and HTTPRoute, only to this designated cluster. The GKE Gateway controller watches the Kubernetes API server of the config cluster for these resources.

To choose a config cluster, consider a regional cluster or another highly available GKE cluster. This helps ensure that updates to your Gateway API resources can be continuously reconciled by the controller.

The multi-cluster Gateway controller uses multi-cluster Services (MCS) to discover and access Kubernetes Services across multiple GKE clusters within a fleet. MCS is a GKE feature that enables service discovery and connectivity between Services that run in different GKE clusters within a fleet.

MCG uses MCS to discover which Services are available in which clusters in order to route external traffic to the Services. The MCG controller uses MCS API resources to group Pods into a single Service that is addressable and spans multiple clusters.

Based on the configurations that you defined in the Gateway API resources, the GKE Gateway controller provides either an external Application Load Balancer or an internal Application Load Balancer. This load balancer serves as the frontend for your application, and distributes traffic directly to the healthy Pods across your fleet, regardless of their location.

The following high-level steps describe the process to deploy a multi-cluster Gateway:

  1. Define a Gateway: in a multi-cluster Gateway setup, you create a Gateway resource that defines the entry point for your traffic in the config cluster. The Gateway resource specifies a GatewayClass, which is a template for a particular type of load balancer, such as a Global external Application Load Balancer or a Regional internal Application Load Balancer. In GKE, the following GatewayClasses deploy multi-cluster Gateways:

    • gke-l7-global-external-managed-mc: provisions a Global external Application Load Balancer.
    • gke-l7-regional-external-managed-mc: provisions a Regional external Application Load Balancer.
    • gke-l7-cross-regional-internal-managed-mc: provisions a Internal Application Load Balancer.
    • gke-l7-rilb-mc: provisions a Internal Application Load Balancer.
    • gke-l7-gxlb-mc: provisions a Classic Application Load Balancer.

    The Gateway also defines how the load balancer listens for incoming traffic by specifying which network listeners (ports and protocols) to expose. For more information about Gateway Classes that GKE supports, see Multi-cluster Services.

  2. Attach HTTPRoutes to the Gateway: HTTPRoute resources define how incoming HTTP/S traffic is routed to specific backend services. HTTPRoutes are attached to Gateway resources and specify rules based on hostnames, paths, headers, and more. HTTPRoute also supports advanced traffic management features like traffic splitting and traffic mirroring.

  3. Create load balancer: when you deploy Gateway and HTTPRoute resources, the GKE Gateway controller interprets these API objects and, in turn, dynamically configures the necessary Google Cloud load balancing infrastructure. The load balancer then directs traffic to the correct Pods, regardless of which cluster the Pods are in. This process provides a highly efficient and scalable way to route traffic.

Traffic flow

The following diagram illustrates how a multi-cluster Gateway works as a centralized load balancer for applications that run across two GKE clusters in different regions:

The load balancer's behavior is configured based on the rules defined in your HTTPRoute resources. When user traffic arrives at the IP address of the provisioned Google Cloud load balancer (as defined by your Gateway resource), the load balancer, which is a Google-managed proxy, routes the traffic. This proxy (either a Google Front End proxy or a regional proxy) directs the traffic to the appropriate backend service endpoint within the correct GKE cluster, based on the following criteria:

  • Health checks
  • Traffic splitting rules
  • Capacity

The traffic flows directly to the optimal Pod in the selected cluster.

What's next

  • Learn how to enable multi-cluster Gateways.
  • Read an overview on how Gateways work in GKE.

Gateway security

This page describes different methods for securing Gateways in Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). You can also learn how to Secure a Gateway.

How Gateway security works

A Gateway represents the frontend of a load balancer. There are two paths that you can secure with authentication and encryption for Gateways:

  • Client to Gateway: traffic originated at the client and terminated at the Gateway.
  • Gateway to Pod: traffic originated at the Gateway and terminated at the backend Pods.

The following diagram shows both paths to authenticate and encrypt Gateways:

In addition to encryption, you can secure the Client-to-Gateway path by using authorization policies. Authorization policies enable a zero-trust architecture by inspecting incoming requests and enforcing access control based on client identities, HTTP headers, and requested paths before the traffic is routed to your backend Pods.

This page describes how to secure the client to Gateway path using certificates uploaded and managed at the Gateway level. To learn how to secure Gateway to Pod traffic, see Secure load balancer to application traffic using TLS.

Benefits

You can secure an application in many different ways using Gateway API, which provides flexibility to different roles interacting with the Gateway.

Who owns domain and TLS configuration?

The Gateway API model introduces two roles that use or deploy Gateways:

  • Platform admin: the cluster operator is the administrator for entire clusters. They manage policies, network access, and application permissions.
  • Application developer: the application developer defines their application and Service configuration.

The following diagram shows the fields in the Gateway and HTTPRoute resources that influence TLS and domain ownership for two applications, store-v1 and store-v2.

In the diagram, the cluster operator controls:

  • Which domains application developers can use for their apps in each namespace.
  • The specific certificates that terminate different domains.
  • Certificates provided by the Gateway owner.
  • Whether HTTPRoute owners can specify their own hostnames for certificate generation.

Application developers control the hostname that generates a certificate, if the Gateway definition permits it.

This separation of operational tasks enables application developers to deploy and manage their own HTTPRoute for more distributed control and lets platform administrators deploy and manage Gateways for centralized control of TLS.

Gateway certificate management

You can secure Gateways using any following methods:

  • Kubernetes Secrets
  • SSL certificates
  • Certificate Manager

If you use Kubernetes Secrets or SslCertificate resources from the Compute Engine API, you can attach at most 15 certificates to a single Gateway.

Certificate Manager lets you attach up to 10,000,000 certificates per load balancer, if you request a quota increase.

To learn more about Google Cloud SSL certificates, see SSL certificates overview.

Kubernetes Secrets

The Gateway API spec supports Kubernetes Secrets for storing and attaching certificates to Gateways. You can associate one or more Kubernetes Secrets with a Gateway using the field Gateway.spec.tls.certificateRef.

Gateway resources secured through Kubernetes Secrets have the following requirements:

  • You must be set the Gateway listener port and protocol to 443 and HTTPS.
  • You must set the listener.tls.mode field to Terminate.
  • You must reference the TLS credentials in the listeners.tls block.

Gateway resources secured using Kubernetes Secrets have the following limitations:

  • Only HTTPS listeners terminate traffic using the specified Secrets, although you can specify multiple listeners with a mix of HTTP and HTTPS.
  • If you have multiple listeners using HTTPS on the same Gateway, each listener must have a unique hostname.
  • You can only omit a single hostname or assign * for each port and protocol pair.
  • You can only assign one default certificate for each Gateway.

To learn how to secure a Gateway using a Kubernetes Secret, see Secure a Gateway using a Kubernetes Secret.

SSL certificates

SSL certificates store and deliver certificates to load balancers. An SSL certificate can be either self-managed or Google-managed.

  • Self-managed SSL certificates are certificates that you obtain, provision, and renew yourself.
  • Google-managed SSL certificates are certificates that Google Cloud obtains, manages, and renews automatically.

To learn more about the differences between these two types of certificates, see SSL certificates overview.

The scope and location of the SSL certificate must match the scope and location of the Gateway that is using it. For example, a global SSL certificate cannot be used by a regional Gateway.

The following table lists the scope and location requirements of SSL certificates for each GatewayClass:

gke-l7-global-external-managed-mc
gke-l7-gxlb
gke-l7-gxlb-mc
gke-l7-regional-external-managed Regional SSL certificate Must be the same region as the Gateway
gke-l7-regional-external-managed-mc
gke-l7-cross-regional-internal-managed-mc
gke-l7-rilb
gke-l7-rilb-mc

Google-managed SSL Certificates aren't compatible with regional Gateways. To secure regional Gateways use Certificate Manager instead.

To learn how to secure a Gateway using an SSL certificate, see Secure a Gateway using an SSL certificate.

Certificate Manager

Certificate Manager is a centralized location to manage your TLS certificates.

When you secure a Gateway using Certificate Manager, you can do the following:

  • Reference a CertificateMap directly from a Gateway that you created in Certificate Manager.
  • Manage your own certificates.
  • Improve certificate propagation times.
  • Use Cloud Monitoring for expired certificates and certificate propagation.

Certificate Manager supports both self-managed and Google-managed SSL certificates. To learn how to secure a Gateway using Certificate Manager, see Secure a Gateway using Certificate Manager.

GatewayClass TLS support

The following table describes the TLS termination methods that GKE supports for each GatewayClass:

Authorization and access control

Preview

This product or feature is subject to the "Pre-GA Offerings Terms" in the General Service Terms section of the Service Specific Terms. Pre-GA products and features are available "as is" and might have limited support. For more information, see the launch stage descriptions.

GKE Gateways support identity-based access control by using the GCPAuthzPolicy custom resource. This resource lets platform administrators define explicit ALLOW or DENY rules for north-south traffic.

Additionally, Gateways can integrate with Service Extensions by using the GCPAuthzExtension resource. This resource enables the Gateway to make inline callouts to external, custom, or third-party authorization engines (such as Identity-Aware Proxy) to evaluate requests in real time.

  • Learn how to deploy Gateways.
  • Learn more about Gateway API concepts.
  • Learn how to configure Gateway resources.

concepts/machine-learning/agent-sandbox:
About Agent Sandbox on GKE

Agent Sandbox on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) helps you run isolated agent workloads in dedicated Kubernetes Pods. Isolation is important when AI agents run untrusted, LLM-generated code. For most agent workloads, you should use Agent Substrate on GKE instead, because it can run more agents on the same nodes. Use Agent Sandbox on GKE when each agent needs a dedicated Pod, GPUs or TPUs, a full Kubernetes PodSpec, or a GKE Autopilot cluster. To compare Agent Sandbox on GKE with Agent Substrate on GKE and choose an architecture for your AI agent workloads, see Plan an architecture for AI agent workloads on GKE.

Agent Sandbox is an open source project under Kubernetes SIG Apps. To use Agent Sandbox on GKE, you install the Agent Sandbox controller on your cluster. You're responsible for upgrading the controller. For instructions, see Install Agent Sandbox on GKE.

This document provides a conceptual overview of Agent Sandbox on GKE.

Why use Agent Sandbox on GKE

Agent Sandbox on GKE gives each agent a dedicated, kernel-isolated Pod that you manage with standard Kubernetes APIs. Key benefits include the following:

  • Kernel-level isolation: Isolates untrusted, LLM-generated code from the node's kernel by using GKE Sandbox with gVisor or microVMs. Agent Sandbox on GKE also works with self-managed open source Kata Containers that you install on your nodes instead of GKE Sandbox. For a tutorial about using open source Kata Containers with Agent Sandbox on GKE, see Enabling Kata Containers on GKE.

    Note: Kata Containers isn't a Google Cloud product. If you install and use this software, then you're responsible for management and troubleshooting. Google's support and SLAs don't apply to Kata Containers.

  • Sub-second provisioning: Provides pre-warmed Pods for your agents, typically in less than one second, instead of waiting for standard Kubernetes Pod scheduling and startup.

  • Cloud-native extensibility: Leverages the power of the Kubernetes paradigm and the managed infrastructure of GKE.

By providing a declarative, standardized API, Agent Sandbox on GKE offers a single-container experience that provides isolation and persistence characteristics similar to a virtual machine (VM), built entirely on Kubernetes primitives.

Common use cases for Agent Sandbox on GKE

Use Agent Sandbox on GKE for workloads that require isolation, persistence, and a stable identity. Example use cases include the following:

  • AI agent runtimes: Run untrusted code in a Pod that uses gVisor or microVMs to isolate the code from the node's kernel.
  • Development environments: Provide developers with persistent, isolated cloud-based coding environments.
  • Notebooks and research tools: Host single-container sessions for interactive tools like Jupyter Notebooks.
  • Stateful single-Pod services: Run applications that need a stable identity and storage without the complexity of a StatefulSet.
  • Programmatic environment management: Use provided client library SDKs, such as the Agent Sandbox Python SDK, to request and manage Sandbox resources directly from your application logic without managing Kubernetes YAML.

How Agent Sandbox on GKE works

Agent Sandbox on GKE uses a custom controller and several Kubernetes Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs) to manage the lifecycle of Sandbox resources.

Core architecture

  • Sandbox custom resource: the primary resource that represents a single, stateful Pod. The resource manages stable hostnames, network identity, and persistent storage. To suspend an idle agent, set the spec.operatingMode field of its Sandbox resource to Suspended. The controller deletes the Pod but keeps the Sandbox resource and its persistent volumes. In-memory data and container file system changes are lost unless you take a Pod snapshot first. To resume the agent, set the field back to Running. Agent Sandbox on GKE doesn't detect idle agents; your application decides when to suspend them.
  • Sandbox Router: a component that provides a stable endpoint and tunnels traffic to the Pods that run your agents, abstracting the underlying networking complexity.
  • Integration with Pod snapshots: Agent Sandbox on GKE integrates with the GKE Pod snapshots feature to suspend and resume workloads by saving and restoring the full state of a container.

Claim model

The claim model is a key feature that separates the user's request for an environment from the specific implementation details, such as where and how the workload is provisioned. Unlike a standard Kubernetes StatefulSet, the claim model lets you request a Sandbox resource without needing to manage the underlying Pod or storage configurations directly.

The claim model uses the SandboxClaim, SandboxWarmPool, and SandboxTemplate custom resources and works as follows:

  1. Users or applications request a Sandbox resource by creating a SandboxClaim resource that references a SandboxWarmPool resource. The warm pool references the SandboxTemplate resource that defines the Pod configuration.
  2. The controller assigns a ready Sandbox resource (and its running Pod) from the warm pool to the claim. If no Sandbox resource in the pool is ready, the controller creates a new Sandbox resource for the claim from the template.

Warm pools

The warm pool feature is designed to minimize startup latency for interactive AI agent scenarios. By using a warm pool, Agent Sandbox on GKE can provide execution environments in less than one second. The feature uses the SandboxWarmPool custom resource and works as follows:

  1. A SandboxWarmPool resource maintains a pool of pre-warmed Sandbox resources with Pods in a ready state.
  2. When a SandboxClaim resource is created, the controller assigns a ready Sandbox resource and its running Pod from the pool instead of waiting for a new Pod to pull images and start.
  3. When combined with Pod snapshots, warm pools can restore Pods from a pre-configured state instead of starting them from scratch.

Network isolation

Agent Sandbox on GKE implements a default deny network policy for the Pods that the controller creates from a SandboxTemplate resource. For each SandboxTemplate resource, the controller creates a NetworkPolicy resource that helps prevent untrusted code inside the Pod from accessing unauthorized internal networks or the GKE control plane. You can define specific network restrictions and allowed egress or ingress rules within your SandboxTemplate resource to control network access for agent workloads.

The controller doesn't create a NetworkPolicy resource for a Sandbox resource that you create directly. To restrict network access for the Pods of these Sandbox resources, create your own NetworkPolicy resource.

Programmatic access with SDKs

AI engineers can consume Agent Sandbox on GKE resources programmatically by using the provided client libraries. For example, the Python SDK provides a high-level interface that creates the underlying SandboxClaim resource for you. The claim references a SandboxWarmPool resource that you create. This interface lets you create and interact with isolated environments directly from your Python-based agent frameworks like LangChain or the Vertex AI Agentic SDK.

Limitations and requirements

Agent Sandbox on GKE has the following limitations and requirements:

  • Cluster version: Agent Sandbox on GKE runs on any supported GKE version. To use Pod snapshots, your cluster must run GKE version 1.35.3-gke.1234000 or later.
  • Infrastructure requirements: Requires the Agent Sandbox controller to be installed and configured on the cluster. Agent Sandbox on GKE doesn't require a specific machine type. For example, the installation guide uses e2-standard-2 nodes. However, Pod snapshots don't support E2 machine types, so if you plan to use Pod snapshots, use another machine series, such as N2.
  • Isolation runtimes: Agent Sandbox on GKE supports gVisor and microVMs as isolation runtimes. Pod snapshots require gVisor and don't work with microVMs. If you don't specify a GKE Sandbox runtime (gVisor or microVMs), your Pods run without kernel isolation, so don't use them to run untrusted code.
  • Hardware accelerators: GPUs and TPUs work only with the gVisor runtime on supported GPU models and TPU versions, and aren't supported with microVMs. In addition, Pod snapshots don't support TPUs.
  • Underlying features availability: Some underlying features, such as GKE Pod snapshots, might be in Preview or have specific regional availability.

What's next

  • Learn how to install Agent Sandbox on GKE.
  • Learn more about isolating AI code execution with Agent Sandbox on GKE.
  • To learn how to use Pod snapshots with Agent Sandbox on GKE, see Save and restore Agent Sandbox on GKE environments with Pod snapshots.
  • Learn about actor-based agent orchestration in About Agent Substrate on GKE.
  • Learn how to use open source Kata Containers with Agent Sandbox on GKE. Kata Containers isn't a Google Cloud product. If you install and use this software, then you're responsible for management and troubleshooting. Google's support and SLAs don't apply to Kata Containers.
  • For the underlying open-source implementation, see the Agent Sandbox GitHub project.
  • For example runtimes and YAML configurations for scenarios such as code execution or computer use, see the Agent Sandbox examples.
  • To interact with Sandbox resources programmatically, see the Agent Sandbox Python SDK README on GitHub.

Save and restore Agent Sandbox on GKE environments with Pod snapshots

This document shows you how to use GKE Pod snapshots to save the state of a running Agent Sandbox on GKE environment.

Agent Sandbox on GKE improves your security by providing an isolated environment for executing untrusted code, such as code generated by large language models (LLMs). Running this type of code directly in a cluster poses security risks, because untrusted code could potentially access or interfere with other apps or the underlying cluster node itself.

GKE Pod snapshots let you save and restore the state of sandboxed environments. This functionality is useful for the following reasons:

  • Fast startup: reduce sandbox startup time by restoring from a pre-warmed snapshot.
  • Long-running agents: pause a sandbox that takes a long time to run and resume it later, or move it to a different node, without losing progress.
  • Stateful workloads: persist the context of an agent, such as conversation history or intermediate calculations, by saving and restoring the state of its sandboxed environment.
  • Reproducibility: capture a specific state and use it as a base to start multiple new sandboxes with the same initialized state.

A snapshot can be triggered in two ways:

  • Manual trigger: you create a PodSnapshotManualTrigger resource to trigger the snapshot.
  • Workload trigger: the sandboxed application itself signals when it's ready to be saved.

This document shows you how to manually trigger a snapshot.

Before you begin

  1. In the Google Cloud console, on the project selector page, select or create a Google Cloud project.

    Roles required to select or create a project

    • Select a project: Selecting a project doesn't require a specific IAM role—you can select any project that you've been granted a role on.
    • Create a project: To create a project, you need the Project Creator role (roles/resourcemanager.projectCreator), which contains the resourcemanager.projects.create permission. Learn how to grant roles.
    Note: If you don't plan to keep the resources that you create in this procedure, create a project instead of selecting an existing project. After you finish these steps, you can delete the project, removing all resources associated with the project.

    Go to project selector

  2. Verify that billing is enabled for your Google Cloud project.

  3. Enable the Google Kubernetes Engine, Cloud Storage, Identity and Access Management (IAM) APIs, if any are not already enabled.

    Roles required to enable APIs

    To enable APIs, you need the serviceusage.services.enable permission. If you created the project, then you likely already have this permission through the Owner role (roles/owner). Otherwise, you can get this permission through the Service Usage Admin role (roles/serviceusage.serviceUsageAdmin). Learn how to grant roles.

    Enable the APIs

  4. In the Google Cloud console, activate Cloud Shell.

    Activate Cloud Shell

Requirements

GKE Pod snapshots requires GKE version 1.35.3-gke.1234000 or later. Both Autopilot and Standard modes are supported.

Pod snapshots require gVisor and don't work with microVM sandboxes.

Because Pod snapshots require GKE Sandbox, your environment is subject to certain limitations. For example, Pod snapshots don't support E2 machine types. Consequently, this tutorial creates a node pool consisting of N2 machines.

For a full list of restrictions, including information on using GPU-based machine types, see Limitations and requirements.

Define environment variables

To simplify the commands that you run in this document, you can set environment variables in Cloud Shell. These variables store values such as the ID of your Google Cloud project, the name of the Cloud Storage bucket that will store your snapshots, and the location of your GKE cluster.

After you define these variables, you can reuse them in multiple commands by referencing the variable name (for example, $CLUSTER_NAME) instead of retyping or replacing values each time. This approach makes the process easier to follow and reduces the risk of errors.

To define the following useful environment variables in Cloud Shell, run the following commands:

export PROJECT_ID=$(gcloud config get project)
export CLUSTER_NAME="agent-sandbox-cluster"
export GKE_LOCATION="us-central1"
export ZONE="us-central1-a"
export AGENT_SANDBOX_VERSION="v1.0.6"
export NODE_POOL_NAME="agent-sandbox-node-pool"
export MACHINE_TYPE="n2-standard-2"
export SNAPSHOTS_BUCKET_NAME="agent-sandbox-snapshots-${PROJECT_ID}"
export SNAPSHOT_NAMESPACE="pod-snapshots-ns"
export SNAPSHOT_KSA_NAME="pod-snapshot-sa"
export SNAPSHOT_FOLDER="my-snapshots"
export PROJECT_NUMBER=$(gcloud projects describe ${PROJECT_ID} --format="value(projectNumber)")

Here's an explanation of these environment variables:

  • PROJECT_ID: the ID of your current Google Cloud project. Commands in this document use this ID to name resources and to grant IAM permissions.
  • CLUSTER_NAME: the name of your GKE cluster (for example, agent-sandbox-cluster).
  • GKE_LOCATION: the Google Cloud region for your Cloud Storage bucket (for example, us-central1). If you create an Autopilot cluster, the cluster also uses this region.
  • ZONE: the zone for your GKE cluster. If you create a Standard cluster, set this to a zone in the GKE_LOCATION region (for example, us-central1-a). To reduce costs, this document creates a zonal Standard cluster.
  • AGENT_SANDBOX_VERSION: the version of the open source Agent Sandbox controller to install. This document uses version 1.0.6.
  • NODE_POOL_NAME: the name of the node pool that will run sandboxed workloads (for example, agent-sandbox-node-pool).
  • MACHINE_TYPE: the machine type of the nodes in your node pool (for example, n2-standard-2). Pod snapshots don't support E2 machine types. If you want to use GPU-based machine types for the nodes in your node pool, see Limitations and requirements. For details about different machine series and choosing between different options, see the Machine families resource and comparison guide.
  • SNAPSHOTS_BUCKET_NAME: the name of the Cloud Storage bucket you will create to store snapshots.
  • SNAPSHOT_NAMESPACE: the Kubernetes namespace where your snapshot workload and service account will reside.
  • SNAPSHOT_KSA_NAME: the name of the Kubernetes service account your workload will use to authenticate.
  • SNAPSHOT_FOLDER: the directory inside your Cloud Storage bucket where snapshots will be organized.
  • PROJECT_NUMBER: the unique numerical identifier for your project, used for IAM permission bindings.

Overview of configuration steps

To enable Pod snapshots of Agent Sandbox on GKE environments, you need to perform some configuration steps. To understand these steps, it's helpful to first understand a few key concepts and then the snapshot process:

Key concepts

  • Environment: a sandboxed application runs inside a Kubernetes Pod on a GKE cluster node.
  • Identity: the Pod is associated with a Kubernetes service account and runs in a special namespace that you create. Together, the Kubernetes service account and the namespace form a unique identity that is used to grant the Pod secure access to Google Cloud resources.
  • Permissions: to allow snapshots to be saved to Cloud Storage, the Pod's identity must be granted specific IAM permissions that allow it to write to a Cloud Storage bucket.

Snapshot process

  1. Trigger: a snapshot is initiated, either manually (externally) or by the sandboxed workload itself. This document demonstrates a manual trigger which you initiate by creating a PodSnapshotManualTrigger resource.
  2. Capture: GKE captures the running state of the Pod, such as the state of the Pod's memory and its file system.
  3. Upload: using the permissions granted to the Pod's Kubernetes service account, GKE uploads the captured state as snapshot files to the designated Cloud Storage bucket.

To learn more about how GKE uses Kubernetes service accounts and IAM roles to access Google Cloud resources, see Authenticate to Google Cloud APIs from GKE workloads.

To enable Pod snapshots of Agent Sandbox on GKE environments, perform the following configuration. First, you prepare a cluster environment by creating a GKE cluster with Workload Identity Federation for GKE and the Pod snapshots features enabled. Next, you configure Cloud Storage and IAM policies to help ensure that your snapshots are stored securely and that your sandbox has the necessary permissions. Finally, you create the snapshot resources that specify the storage location and policies for your sandbox.

The following table summarizes the configuration steps you need to perform, and each step is explained in the sections that follow:

Topic Task
Cluster setup 1. Create a GKE cluster and enable the Pod snapshots and Workload Identity Federation for GKE features.
2. Deploy Agent Sandbox.
Configure storage and permissions 1. Create the Cloud Storage bucket and managed folder.
2. Create the custom IAM role.
3. Create the Kubernetes namespace and the Kubernetes service account (KSA).
4. Bind the IAM role to the Kubernetes service account.
5. Grant permissions to the snapshot controller.
Configure snapshot resources 1. Create a PodSnapshotStorageConfig resource
2. Create a PodSnapshotPolicy resource
3. Create SandboxTemplate, SandboxWarmPool, and SandboxClaim resources

Cluster setup

A sandboxed app runs inside a Pod on a GKE cluster node, so you need to set up a cluster environment. This section shows you how to create a GKE cluster, and deploy the Agent Sandbox controller.

Create a new GKE cluster that meets the requirements

Create a new GKE cluster with Pod snapshots enabled. Pod snapshots require GKE version 1.35.3-gke.1234000 or later. The following commands enroll the cluster in the Rapid release channel, whose default version meets this requirement:

Autopilot

Create an Autopilot cluster with the required features:

gcloud container clusters create-auto ${CLUSTER_NAME} \
   --release-channel=rapid \
   --enable-pod-snapshots \
   --location=${GKE_LOCATION}

Standard

Create a Standard cluster with the required features. To reduce costs, the following command creates a zonal cluster, which runs its control plane and nodes in one zone:

gcloud container clusters create ${CLUSTER_NAME} \
   --release-channel=rapid \
   --enable-pod-snapshots \
   --machine-type=${MACHINE_TYPE} \
   --workload-pool=${PROJECT_ID}.svc.id.goog \
   --workload-metadata=GKE_METADATA \
   --num-nodes=1 \
   --location=${ZONE}

Create a node pool with GKE Sandbox enabled. GKE Sandbox is a container security feature based on the open-source gVisor project that provides an additional layer of isolation between running applications and the host operating system:

gcloud container node-pools create ${NODE_POOL_NAME} \
   --cluster ${CLUSTER_NAME} \
   --num-nodes=1 \
   --location=${ZONE} \
   --project=${PROJECT_ID} \
   --machine-type=${MACHINE_TYPE} \
   --sandbox type=gvisor

Retrieve credentials

Retrieve the cluster's credentials so that the kubectl CLI can connect to the cluster:

Autopilot

gcloud container clusters get-credentials ${CLUSTER_NAME} \
    --location=${GKE_LOCATION}

Standard

gcloud container clusters get-credentials ${CLUSTER_NAME} \
    --location=${ZONE}

Deploy the Agent Sandbox Controller to your cluster

You can deploy the Agent Sandbox controller and its required components by applying the official release manifest to your cluster. This manifest is a configuration file that instructs Kubernetes to download all the necessary components that are required to deploy and run the Agent Sandbox controller on your cluster.

To deploy Agent Sandbox to your GKE cluster, run the following command:

# Apply the release manifest for the controller and its CustomResourceDefinitions
kubectl apply -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/releases/download/${AGENT_SANDBOX_VERSION}/sandbox-with-extensions.yaml

For more information about installing Agent Sandbox, see Install Agent Sandbox on GKE.

Verify the controller

After applying the manifest, check that the Agent Sandbox controller Pod is running correctly in the agent-sandbox-system namespace. The manifest automatically created the agent-sandbox-system namespace when you applied it in the previous step.

kubectl get pods -n agent-sandbox-system

Wait for the Pod to show 'Running' in the STATUS column and '1/1' in the READY column. When the Pod is running correctly, the output looks similar to this:

NAME                                        READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
agent-sandbox-controller-7d5c9b8f6d-x2k9p   1/1     Running   0          2m

Now that the Agent Sandbox controller is running, it can automatically create and manage sandboxed environments for any Sandbox resources that you create in your cluster.

Configure storage and permissions

This section shows you how to configure the storage and permissions required for Pod snapshots. You create a Cloud Storage bucket and a managed folder to store the snapshot data. Then, you grant your sandbox and the snapshot controller the permissions they need to access that storage.

Create the Cloud Storage bucket

Create a bucket to store your snapshots. To help ensure that the snapshot process is fast and cost-effective, create the bucket with the following settings:

  • Enable hierarchical namespaces: the hierarchical namespaces feature organizes your bucket into a file system hierarchy rather than a flat namespace. This configuration allows for higher read and write throughput, and consequently speeds up saving and restoring snapshots.
  • Disable soft delete: the soft delete feature protects data by retaining deleted files for a set period. However, the snapshot process creates and deletes many temporary files during upload. Disable soft delete to avoid unnecessary charges for storing these temporary files.

To create the bucket with these settings, run the following command:

gcloud storage buckets create "gs://${SNAPSHOTS_BUCKET_NAME}" \
    --uniform-bucket-level-access \
    --enable-hierarchical-namespace \
    --soft-delete-duration=0d \
    --location="${GKE_LOCATION}"

Create a managed folder

Create a managed folder to organize snapshots within your bucket. Managed folders allow you to apply IAM permissions to a specific folder rather than to the entire bucket. This folder-level access limits your sandbox's access to only its own snapshots, and isolates those snapshots from other data in the bucket.

To create a managed folder, run this command:

gcloud storage managed-folders create "gs://${SNAPSHOTS_BUCKET_NAME}/${SNAPSHOT_FOLDER}/"

Configure the service account and IAM roles

To allow GKE to save snapshots securely, the Kubernetes service account used by the Pods running your sandboxed workload needs permission to write to your bucket. You grant this permission by binding Google Cloud IAM roles to the Kubernetes service account used by the Pods. This section shows you how to create a custom IAM role, create the Kubernetes service account, and configure the necessary permissions.

  1. Create a custom IAM role called podSnapshotGcsReadWriter that contains the permissions required to write snapshot data. If this role already exists in your project, for example from an earlier run of this document, skip this step. Otherwise, run the following command:

    gcloud iam roles create podSnapshotGcsReadWriter \
    --project="${PROJECT_ID}" \
    --permissions="storage.objects.get,storage.objects.create,storage.objects.delete,storage.folders.create"

    When the role is created successfully, the output looks like this:

    Created role [podSnapshotGcsReadWriter].
etag: BwZJUfjNbew=
includedPermissions:
- storage.folders.create
- storage.objects.create
- storage.objects.delete
- storage.objects.get
name: projects/${PROJECT_ID}/roles/podSnapshotGcsReadWriter
stage: ALPHA
title: podSnapshotGcsReadWriter

    If the command fails with a FAILED_PRECONDITION error that says the role ID has been marked for deletion, you deleted a role with this ID recently, for example in the clean-up steps of an earlier run of this document. IAM doesn't let you reuse that ID for up to 37 days. Run the command again with a different role ID, such as podSnapshotGcsReadWriter2, and use that ID instead of podSnapshotGcsReadWriter in the rest of this document.

  2. Create the namespace in which your sandbox and its service account will reside:

    kubectl create namespace "${SNAPSHOT_NAMESPACE}"

  3. Create the Kubernetes service account in the namespace you just created. Together, the Kubernetes service account and the namespace form a unique identity used to grant your sandbox secure access to Google Cloud resources:

    kubectl create serviceaccount "${SNAPSHOT_KSA_NAME}" \
    --namespace "${SNAPSHOT_NAMESPACE}"

  4. Grant the roles/storage.bucketViewer role to all service accounts in the namespace. This role allows the accounts to view the bucket's metadata but not to read or write the data itself:

    gcloud storage buckets add-iam-policy-binding "gs://${SNAPSHOTS_BUCKET_NAME}" \
    --member="principalSet://iam.googleapis.com/projects/${PROJECT_NUMBER}/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/${PROJECT_ID}.svc.id.goog/namespace/${SNAPSHOT_NAMESPACE}" \
    --role="roles/storage.bucketViewer"

  5. Grant your custom podSnapshotGcsReadWriter role to the Kubernetes service account for your sandbox. This binding allows only this specific account to write data to the managed folder. A new custom role can take a few minutes to become available, so if this command fails because the role doesn't exist, wait a minute and then run the command again:

    gcloud storage buckets add-iam-policy-binding "gs://${SNAPSHOTS_BUCKET_NAME}" \
    --member="principal://iam.googleapis.com/projects/${PROJECT_NUMBER}/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/${PROJECT_ID}.svc.id.goog/subject/ns/${SNAPSHOT_NAMESPACE}/sa/${SNAPSHOT_KSA_NAME}" \
    --role="projects/${PROJECT_ID}/roles/podSnapshotGcsReadWriter"

  6. Grant the roles/storage.objectUser role to the Kubernetes service account. This role is required for the Pod snapshot agent to perform operations on managed folders:

    gcloud storage buckets add-iam-policy-binding "gs://${SNAPSHOTS_BUCKET_NAME}" \
    --member="principal://iam.googleapis.com/projects/${PROJECT_NUMBER}/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/${PROJECT_ID}.svc.id.goog/subject/ns/${SNAPSHOT_NAMESPACE}/sa/${SNAPSHOT_KSA_NAME}" \
    --role="roles/storage.objectUser"

Grant permissions to the snapshot controller

Grant the objectUser role to the GKE system's snapshot controller. This permission allows the controller to manage the snapshot lifecycle, such as deleting snapshot objects when you delete a PodSnapshot resource:

gcloud storage buckets add-iam-policy-binding "gs://${SNAPSHOTS_BUCKET_NAME}" \
    --member="serviceAccount:service-${PROJECT_NUMBER}@container-engine-robot.iam.gserviceaccount.com" \
    --role="roles/storage.objectUser"

Configure snapshot resources

This section shows you how to configure the snapshot resources for your Agent Sandbox on GKE workload.

Define snapshot storage and rules

To specify where GKE saves your snapshots and which rules govern the snapshot process, you create two custom resources:

  • PodSnapshotStorageConfig: this resource specifies the Cloud Storage bucket and folder location where GKE saves your snapshot files.
  • PodSnapshotPolicy: this resource defines which Pods are eligible for snapshots based on their Kubernetes labels. It also specifies the trigger rules, such as whether snapshots are manual or initiated by the sandbox workload. This example groups snapshots by the agents.x-k8s.io/sandbox-name-hash label, which the Agent Sandbox controller adds to the Pod of each sandbox. This grouping means that GKE restores each sandbox only from its own snapshots.

To apply both resources in one step, run the following command in Cloud Shell. This method helps to ensure that your environment variables are correctly injected:

kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: podsnapshot.gke.io/v1
kind: PodSnapshotStorageConfig
metadata:
  name: cpu-pssc-gcs
spec:
  snapshotStorageConfig:
    gcs:
      bucket: "${SNAPSHOTS_BUCKET_NAME}"
      path: "${SNAPSHOT_FOLDER}"
EOF

sleep 5

kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: podsnapshot.gke.io/v1
kind: PodSnapshotPolicy
metadata:
  name: cpu-psp
  namespace: ${SNAPSHOT_NAMESPACE}
spec:
  storageConfigName: cpu-pssc-gcs
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: agent-sandbox-workload
  triggerConfig:
    type: manual
    postCheckpoint: resume
  snapshotGroupingRules:
    groupByLabelValue:
      labels:
      - agents.x-k8s.io/sandbox-name-hash
EOF

Verify the configuration

After you apply the snapshot storage configuration and policy, verify that the resources are ready to use. This section shows you how to check the status of these custom resources.

  1. Check the status of the PodSnapshotStorageConfig resource:

    kubectl get podsnapshotstorageconfigs.podsnapshot.gke.io cpu-pssc-gcs -o yaml

    The output should contain a condition with type: Ready and status: "True":

    status:
  conditions:
  - lastTransitionTime: "2025-10-31T18:18:02Z"
    message: Valid PodSnapshotStorageConfig
    reason: StorageConfigValid
    status: "True"
    type: Ready

  2. Check the status of the PodSnapshotPolicy resource:

    kubectl get podsnapshotpolicies.podsnapshot.gke.io cpu-psp \
  --namespace "${SNAPSHOT_NAMESPACE}" -o yaml

    The output should contain a condition with type: Ready and status: "True". It should also indicate that the referenced PodSnapshotStorageConfig resource was found:

    status:
  conditions:
  - lastTransitionTime: "2025-10-31T18:19:47Z"
    message: The referenced PodSnapshotStorageConfig "cpu-pssc-gcs" was found
    reason: StorageConfigValid
    status: "True"
    type: Ready

Create the sandbox template

Now that the storage policies and permissions are in place, you create the SandboxTemplate, SandboxWarmPool, and SandboxClaim resources. The SandboxWarmPool resource keeps a pre-warmed sandbox running, and the SandboxClaim resource claims that sandbox from the pool. For the snapshot process to work, the sandbox must run with the Kubernetes service account you created earlier in this document. The sandbox must also have the labels that you specified earlier in the PodSnapshotPolicy resource.

This example uses a Python app that prints an incrementing counter to the logs. This counter lets you verify that the state is successfully saved and restored later.

Autopilot

Pod snapshots don't support E2 machine types. In Autopilot, GKE might default to machine types that don't support Pod snapshots. To help ensure your workloads run on compatible hardware, you should use a custom ComputeClass to prioritize compatible machine families.

  1. Save the following manifest as non-e2-class.yaml:

    apiVersion: cloud.google.com/v1
kind: ComputeClass
metadata:
  name: non-e2-class
spec:
  priorities:
  - machineFamily: n2
  - machineFamily: c3
  activeMigration:
    optimizeRulePriority: false
  whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotScaleUp

  2. Apply the manifest:

    kubectl apply -f non-e2-class.yaml

  3. To create the SandboxTemplate and SandboxWarmPool resources, apply the following manifest. Notice that the SandboxTemplate resource refers to the ComputeClass you just created using the cloud.google.com/compute-class: non-e2-class node selector.

    kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
---
apiVersion: extensions.agents.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: SandboxTemplate
metadata:
  name: python-runtime-template
  namespace: ${SNAPSHOT_NAMESPACE}
spec:
  podTemplate:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: agent-sandbox-workload
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: ${SNAPSHOT_KSA_NAME}
      runtimeClassName: gvisor
      nodeSelector:
        cloud.google.com/compute-class: non-e2-class
      containers:
      - name: my-container
        image: python:3.10-slim
        command: ["python3", "-c"]
        args:
          - |
            import time
            i = 0
            while True:
              print(f"Count: {i}", flush=True)
              i += 1
              time.sleep(1)
---
apiVersion: extensions.agents.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: SandboxWarmPool
metadata:
  name: python-sandbox-warmpool
  namespace: ${SNAPSHOT_NAMESPACE}
spec:
  replicas: 1
  sandboxTemplateRef:
    name: python-runtime-template
EOF

Standard

To create the SandboxTemplate and SandboxWarmPool resources, apply the following manifest:

kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
---
apiVersion: extensions.agents.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: SandboxTemplate
metadata:
  name: python-runtime-template
  namespace: ${SNAPSHOT_NAMESPACE}
spec:
  podTemplate:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: agent-sandbox-workload
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: ${SNAPSHOT_KSA_NAME}
      runtimeClassName: gvisor
      containers:
      - name: my-container
        image: python:3.10-slim
        command: ["python3", "-c"]
        args:
          - |
            import time
            i = 0
            while True:
              print(f"Count: {i}", flush=True)
              i += 1
              time.sleep(1)
---
apiVersion: extensions.agents.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: SandboxWarmPool
metadata:
  name: python-sandbox-warmpool
  namespace: ${SNAPSHOT_NAMESPACE}
spec:
  replicas: 1
  sandboxTemplateRef:
    name: python-runtime-template
EOF

After you create the resources, claim a sandbox from the warm pool:

  1. Wait until the warm pool's sandbox is ready:

    kubectl wait sandboxwarmpool python-sandbox-warmpool \
  --namespace "${SNAPSHOT_NAMESPACE}" \
  --for=jsonpath='{.status.readyReplicas}'=1 \
  --timeout=600s

  2. Create a SandboxClaim resource that claims the sandbox from the warm pool:

    kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: extensions.agents.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: SandboxClaim
metadata:
  name: python-sandbox-example
  namespace: ${SNAPSHOT_NAMESPACE}
spec:
  warmPoolRef:
    name: python-sandbox-warmpool
EOF

  3. Wait until the claim is ready, and then save the name of the sandbox that the claim uses. The sandbox's Pod has the same name as the sandbox:

    kubectl wait sandboxclaim python-sandbox-example \
  --namespace "${SNAPSHOT_NAMESPACE}" \
  --for=condition=Ready \
  --timeout=300s

export SANDBOX_NAME=$(kubectl get sandboxclaim python-sandbox-example \
  --namespace "${SNAPSHOT_NAMESPACE}" \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.sandbox.name}')
echo "${SANDBOX_NAME}"

Your sandbox is now running with the correct identity and is ready to be snapshotted.

Create a snapshot

This section shows you how to manually trigger a snapshot of your running sandbox. You create a trigger resource that targets your sandbox Pod and then you verify that the snapshot process completes successfully.

  1. Check the initial counter logs: Before triggering the snapshot, view the logs of the running sandbox to see the current counter value. Viewing the logs establishes a baseline to compare against after restoring.

    kubectl logs "${SANDBOX_NAME}" --namespace "${SNAPSHOT_NAMESPACE}" --tail=5

    The output shows the last few lines of the counter, for example:

    Count: 15
Count: 16
Count: 17

    Note the last few "Count" values printed.

  2. Create a PodSnapshotManualTrigger resource: Initiate the snapshot:

    kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: podsnapshot.gke.io/v1
kind: PodSnapshotManualTrigger
metadata:
  name: cpu-snapshot-trigger
  namespace: ${SNAPSHOT_NAMESPACE}
spec:
  targetPod: ${SANDBOX_NAME}
EOF

  3. Verify that the manual trigger was successful:

    kubectl get podsnapshotmanualtriggers.podsnapshot.gke.io \
  --namespace "${SNAPSHOT_NAMESPACE}"

    The output should show a status of Complete, indicating that GKE successfully triggered the snapshot of the target Pod:

    NAME                   TARGET POD                      STATUS     AGE
cpu-snapshot-trigger   python-sandbox-warmpool-x7k2p   Complete   XXs

  4. View more details about the captured state by describing the trigger:

    kubectl describe podsnapshotmanualtriggers.podsnapshot.gke.io cpu-snapshot-trigger \
  --namespace "${SNAPSHOT_NAMESPACE}"

    The output contains a Snapshot Created section with the unique name of the snapshot files stored in your bucket:

    Status:
  Conditions:
    Last Transition Time:  2026-01-30T19:11:04Z
    Message:               checkpoint completed successfully
    Reason:                Complete
    Status:                True
    Type:                  Triggered
  Observed Generation:     1
  Snapshot Created:
    Name:  <UNIQUE_SNAPSHOT_NAME>

Restore from a snapshot

After you capture a snapshot, you can suspend the sandbox to free up its compute resources, and later resume the sandbox from its saved state. When you suspend a sandbox, the Agent Sandbox controller deletes the sandbox's Pod but keeps the Sandbox resource. When you resume the sandbox, the controller re-creates the Pod, and the Pod snapshot controller automatically restores the Pod from the most recent snapshot of that sandbox.

  1. Wait until the snapshot is ready. GKE restores a Pod only from a snapshot that's ready. If you suspend the sandbox before the snapshot is ready, the sandbox starts without the saved state when you resume it.

    export SNAPSHOT_NAME=$(kubectl get podsnapshotmanualtriggers.podsnapshot.gke.io cpu-snapshot-trigger \
  --namespace "${SNAPSHOT_NAMESPACE}" \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.snapshotCreated.name}')

kubectl wait podsnapshots.podsnapshot.gke.io "${SNAPSHOT_NAME}" \
  --namespace "${SNAPSHOT_NAMESPACE}" \
  --for=condition=Ready \
  --timeout=600s

  2. To suspend the sandbox, set its operatingMode field to Suspended, and then wait until the controller deletes the sandbox's Pod:

    kubectl patch sandbox "${SANDBOX_NAME}" \
  --namespace "${SNAPSHOT_NAMESPACE}" \
  --type=merge \
  -p '{"spec":{"operatingMode":"Suspended"}}'

kubectl wait pod "${SANDBOX_NAME}" \
  --namespace "${SNAPSHOT_NAMESPACE}" \
  --for=delete \
  --timeout=120s

  3. To resume the sandbox, set its operatingMode field to Running, and then wait until the sandbox is ready:

    kubectl patch sandbox "${SANDBOX_NAME}" \
  --namespace "${SNAPSHOT_NAMESPACE}" \
  --type=merge \
  -p '{"spec":{"operatingMode":"Running"}}'

kubectl wait sandbox "${SANDBOX_NAME}" \
  --namespace "${SNAPSHOT_NAMESPACE}" \
  --for=condition=Ready \
  --timeout=300s

  4. Verify that the restore took place by viewing the logs. Note that the counter continues from the point where the snapshot was taken:

    kubectl logs "${SANDBOX_NAME}" --namespace "${SNAPSHOT_NAMESPACE}"

    The output should show the counter resuming, for example:

    Count: 18
Count: 19
Count: 20
Count: 21

    If the counter starts from 0 instead, the Pod started without restoring from the snapshot.

Clean up resources

To avoid incurring charges to your Google Cloud account for the resources used in this document, perform the following steps in order to delete the resources you created:

  1. Delete the sandbox claims and warm pools to stop any running Pods and allow the Agent Sandbox controller to gracefully terminate the containers.

    kubectl delete sandboxclaims --all --namespace "${SNAPSHOT_NAMESPACE}"
kubectl delete sandboxwarmpools --all --namespace "${SNAPSHOT_NAMESPACE}"

  2. Delete the sandbox templates and manual triggers used to create sandboxes and initiate snapshots.

    # Delete the blueprints
kubectl delete sandboxtemplates --all --namespace "${SNAPSHOT_NAMESPACE}"

# Delete the snapshot initiation objects
kubectl delete podsnapshotmanualtriggers --all --namespace "${SNAPSHOT_NAMESPACE}"

  3. Delete the snapshot policies that define which Pods are eligible for snapshots within your namespace.

    kubectl delete podsnapshotpolicy cpu-psp --namespace "${SNAPSHOT_NAMESPACE}"

  4. Delete the snapshot storage configuration, which is the global definition of your snapshot storage backend. Because this resource is cluster-scoped, don't use a namespace flag.

    kubectl delete podsnapshotstorageconfig cpu-pssc-gcs

  5. If you created one for Autopilot, delete the ComputeClass.

    kubectl delete computeclass non-e2-class

  6. Delete the Kubernetes namespace to automatically remove the Kubernetes service account and any remaining namespaced metadata.

    kubectl delete namespace "${SNAPSHOT_NAMESPACE}"

  7. Delete the GKE cluster to remove the underlying infrastructure and all nodes associated with the tutorial.

    Autopilot

    gcloud container clusters delete "${CLUSTER_NAME}" \
    --location="${GKE_LOCATION}" --quiet

    Standard

    gcloud container clusters delete "${CLUSTER_NAME}" \
    --location="${ZONE}" --quiet

  8. Delete the Cloud Storage bucket (optional) by using the recursive remove command if you want to fully reset your storage. Note that you can skip this if you intend to reuse your correctly configured bucket for future tests.

    gcloud storage rm --recursive "gs://${SNAPSHOTS_BUCKET_NAME:?Error: SNAPSHOTS_BUCKET_NAME is not set. Please re-define the environment variables you defined earlier.}"

  9. Delete the custom IAM role (optional) if you want to return your project to a completely clean state. Because IAM roles persist even after the cluster is deleted, you must delete them separately.

    gcloud iam roles delete podSnapshotGcsReadWriter --project="${PROJECT_ID}"

What's next

  • Learn more about GKE Pod Snapshots.
  • Learn more about the Agent Sandbox open-source project on GitHub.
  • Learn how to Isolate AI code execution with Agent Sandbox on GKE.

how-to/how-install-agent-sandbox:
Install Agent Sandbox on GKE

This document explains how to install the open source Agent Sandbox controller on a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster to run isolated agent workloads in dedicated Kubernetes Pods. You also learn how to create a Sandbox resource that runs untrusted code in the gVisor runtime. For most agent workloads, use Agent Substrate on GKE instead, because it can run more agents on the same nodes. Use Agent Sandbox on GKE when each agent needs a dedicated Pod, GPUs or TPUs, a full Kubernetes PodSpec, or a GKE Autopilot cluster. To compare Agent Sandbox on GKE with Agent Substrate on GKE and choose an architecture for your AI agent workloads, see Plan an architecture for AI agent workloads on GKE.

For an overview of how Agent Sandbox on GKE isolates untrusted AI-generated code, see About Agent Sandbox on GKE.

Costs

Agent Sandbox on GKE is open source software that you can use at no extra charge. GKE pricing applies to the resources that you create, including the compute resources that the Agent Sandbox controller uses.

To avoid unnecessary charges, ensure that you disable GKE or delete the project after you have completed this document.

Before you begin

  1. In the Google Cloud console, on the project selector page, select or create a Google Cloud project.

    Roles required to select or create a project

    • Select a project: Selecting a project doesn't require a specific IAM role—you can select any project that you've been granted a role on.
    • Create a project: To create a project, you need the Project Creator role (roles/resourcemanager.projectCreator), which contains the resourcemanager.projects.create permission. Learn how to grant roles.
    Note: If you don't plan to keep the resources that you create in this procedure, create a project instead of selecting an existing project. After you finish these steps, you can delete the project, removing all resources associated with the project.

    Go to project selector

  2. Verify that billing is enabled for your Google Cloud project.

  3. Enable the Google Kubernetes Engine API, if it is not already enabled.

    Roles required to enable APIs

    To enable APIs, you need the serviceusage.services.enable permission. If you created the project, then you likely already have this permission through the Owner role (roles/owner). Otherwise, you can get this permission through the Service Usage Admin role (roles/serviceusage.serviceUsageAdmin). Learn how to grant roles.

    Enable the API

  4. In the Google Cloud console, activate Cloud Shell.

    Activate Cloud Shell

Define environment variables

To simplify the commands that you run in this document, you can set environment variables in Cloud Shell. In Cloud Shell, define the following useful environment variables by running the following commands:

export CLUSTER_NAME="agent-sandbox-cluster"
export LOCATION="us-central1"
export AGENT_SANDBOX_VERSION="v1.0.6"
export NODE_POOL_NAME="agent-sandbox-pool"
export MACHINE_TYPE="e2-standard-2"

Here's an explanation of these environment variables:

  • CLUSTER_NAME: the name of your GKE cluster—for example, agent-sandbox-cluster.
  • LOCATION: the Google Cloud region or zone where your GKE cluster is created. If you create an Autopilot cluster, set this to the region (for example, us-central1). Autopilot clusters are always regional. If you create a Standard cluster, set this to the zone (for example, us-central1-a). To reduce costs, this document creates a zonal cluster, which uses fewer nodes than a regional cluster.
  • AGENT_SANDBOX_VERSION: the version of the open source Agent Sandbox controller to install. This document uses version 1.0.6. To see other versions, go to the Agent Sandbox releases page.
  • NODE_POOL_NAME: the name of the node pool that will run your agent Pods—for example, agent-sandbox-pool. This variable is only required if you are creating a GKE Standard cluster.
  • MACHINE_TYPE: the machine type of the nodes in your cluster's default node pool and in the gVisor node pool—for example, e2-standard-2. For details about different machine series and choosing between different options, see the Machine families resource and comparison guide. This variable is only required if you are creating a GKE Standard cluster.

Create a GKE cluster

Agent Sandbox on GKE isolates agent workloads by using GKE Sandbox with gVisor or microVMs. If you don't specify a GKE Sandbox runtime (gVisor or microVMs), your Pods run without kernel isolation, so don't use them to run untrusted code. This document uses gVisor. Autopilot clusters enable gVisor automatically. In Standard clusters, you create a node pool that has gVisor enabled. To use microVMs instead, see Enable the microVM sandbox type. The recommended security policy allows only gVisor, so it rejects Sandbox resources that use microVMs.

Best practice:

Use an Autopilot cluster for a fully managed Kubernetes experience. To choose the GKE mode of operation that's the best fit for your workloads, see Choose a GKE mode of operation.

Autopilot

To create an Autopilot cluster, make sure that the LOCATION environment variable is set to a region, such as us-central1, and then run the following command:

gcloud container clusters create-auto ${CLUSTER_NAME} \
    --location=${LOCATION}

Standard

To create a Standard cluster, you create the cluster and then add a node pool with gVisor enabled. To reduce costs, this document creates a zonal cluster with a single node per pool.

Best practice:

Use a regional cluster for production workloads. Regional clusters replicate the control plane and nodes across multiple zones, which provides higher availability than zonal clusters.

  1. Set the LOCATION environment variable to a zone, such as us-central1-a:

    export LOCATION="us-central1-a"

  2. Create the cluster:

    gcloud container clusters create ${CLUSTER_NAME} \
    --location=${LOCATION} \
    --machine-type=${MACHINE_TYPE} \
    --num-nodes=1

  3. Create a separate node pool with gVisor enabled:

    gcloud container node-pools create ${NODE_POOL_NAME} \
    --cluster=${CLUSTER_NAME} \
    --machine-type=${MACHINE_TYPE} \
    --location=${LOCATION} \
    --num-nodes=1 \
    --image-type=cos_containerd \
    --sandbox=type=gvisor

    To use microVMs instead of gVisor, create the node pool as described in Enable the microVM sandbox type. The rest of this document uses gVisor.

To use an existing Standard cluster instead, make sure that the cluster includes a node pool that has gVisor enabled. If the cluster doesn't have such a node pool, create one by running the preceding gcloud container node-pools create command.

To enable the kubectl command-line tool to connect to the cluster, get the cluster credentials:

gcloud container clusters get-credentials ${CLUSTER_NAME} \
    --location=${LOCATION}

Install Agent Sandbox

To install Agent Sandbox, apply a release manifest from the Agent Sandbox GitHub repository. The sandbox-with-extensions.yaml manifest installs the Agent Sandbox controller and the CustomResourceDefinitions for the Sandbox resource and for the SandboxTemplate, SandboxClaim, and SandboxWarmPool extension resources.

  1. Apply the release manifest:

    kubectl apply -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/releases/download/${AGENT_SANDBOX_VERSION}/sandbox-with-extensions.yaml

    The manifest creates the agent-sandbox-system namespace and deploys the controller in that namespace.

  2. Wait until the controller is ready:

    kubectl rollout status deployment/agent-sandbox-controller \
    --namespace=agent-sandbox-system \
    --timeout=120s
    Note: In an Autopilot cluster, the controller can take several minutes to become ready because GKE might need to create a node for it. If the command times out before the controller is ready, run the command again.

You can also install Agent Sandbox by using Helm. For instructions, see the Agent Sandbox Helm chart README.

Verify the installation

  1. Verify that the Agent Sandbox CustomResourceDefinitions are installed:

    kubectl get crd \
    sandboxes.agents.x-k8s.io \
    sandboxtemplates.extensions.agents.x-k8s.io \
    sandboxclaims.extensions.agents.x-k8s.io \
    sandboxwarmpools.extensions.agents.x-k8s.io

    The output lists the four CustomResourceDefinitions.

  2. Verify that the controller is running:

    kubectl get deployment agent-sandbox-controller \
    --namespace=agent-sandbox-system

    When the controller is running, the READY column shows 1/1.

Apply the recommended security policy

By default, Agent Sandbox on GKE doesn't restrict the configuration of the Pods that run your agents. To help enforce isolation settings for your agent Pods, apply the recommended secure-sandbox-policy ValidatingAdmissionPolicy from the Agent Sandbox GitHub repository. This policy rejects any Sandbox resource that doesn't meet the Agent Sandbox on GKE deployment requirements.

  1. Apply the policy:

    kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/${AGENT_SANDBOX_VERSION}/examples/policy/vap/secure-sandbox-policy.yaml

  2. Apply the policy binding. The binding enforces the policy in all namespaces except system namespaces, such as kube-system:

    kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/${AGENT_SANDBOX_VERSION}/examples/policy/vap/secure-sandbox-binding.yaml

The policy validates Sandbox resources. When you create a SandboxWarmPool resource or a SandboxClaim resource, the controller creates Sandbox resources from a SandboxTemplate resource. If the template doesn't meet the requirements, the policy rejects the Sandbox resource, and the error appears in the controller logs. To view the logs, run the following command:

kubectl logs deployment/agent-sandbox-controller \
    --namespace=agent-sandbox-system

You own this policy, and you can modify it to fit your workloads. For more information, see Sandbox security policies.

Agent Sandbox on GKE deployment requirements

If you apply the recommended security policy, your workload manifests, such as a Sandbox or SandboxTemplate resource, must include specific security and configuration settings. If a Sandbox resource doesn't meet these requirements, the admission controller rejects it. The container requirements apply to all containers in the Pod, including init containers and ephemeral containers.

Required configuration

Your deployment manifest must include the following settings:

  • runtimeClassName: gvisor: runs the Pod in the gVisor runtime of GKE Sandbox. The policy rejects Sandbox resources that use any other runtime, including microVMs.
  • automountServiceAccountToken: false: prevents the Pod from automatically mounting the default service account token.
  • securityContext.runAsNonRoot: true: ensures the container does not run as the root user.
  • securityContext.capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]: drops all Linux capabilities from the container.
  • resources.limits: you must specify CPU and memory limits to prevent potential denial-of-service (DoS) scenarios.
  • nodeSelector: must target sandbox.gke.io/runtime: gvisor.
  • tolerations: must include a toleration for the sandbox.gke.io/runtime=gvisor:NoSchedule taint.

Prohibited configuration

Your deployment manifest must not include any of the following:

  • hostNetwork: true, hostPID: true, or hostIPC: true.
  • privileged: true in container security contexts.
  • procMount: Unmasked in container security contexts.
  • HostPath volumes.
  • Added capabilities (capabilities.add).
  • hostPort settings.
  • Custom sysctls.
  • Projected volumes for service account tokens or certificates.

Deploy the Sandbox Router (optional)

The Sandbox Router is an HTTP proxy that routes requests from clients, such as the Agent Sandbox Python client, to the Pods that run your agents. If you plan to use the Python client, for example as described in Isolate AI code execution with Agent Sandbox on GKE, deploy the router.

You deploy the router in the agent-sandbox-system namespace. By default, the network policy that Agent Sandbox on GKE creates for each SandboxTemplate resource allows incoming traffic to agent Pods only from the router Pods in this namespace.

  1. Create the router's service account and the RBAC permissions that let the router look up agent Pods:

    kubectl apply \
    -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/${AGENT_SANDBOX_VERSION}/sandbox-router/deploy/serviceaccount.yaml \
    -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/${AGENT_SANDBOX_VERSION}/sandbox-router/deploy/rbac.yaml

  2. Deploy the router. The following command sets the router image to the same version as the controller:

    curl -sSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/${AGENT_SANDBOX_VERSION}/sandbox-router/deploy/deployment.yaml \
    | sed "s|sandbox-router-go:latest|sandbox-router-go:${AGENT_SANDBOX_VERSION}|" \
    | kubectl apply -f -

  3. Create the router's Service:

    kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/${AGENT_SANDBOX_VERSION}/sandbox-router/deploy/service.yaml

  4. Wait until the router is ready:

    kubectl rollout status deployment/sandbox-router \
    --namespace=agent-sandbox-system \
    --timeout=120s

This router configuration is for development and testing. For production settings, such as TLS, replica counts, and network policies for the router, see the Sandbox Router deployment README.

Deploy a sandboxed environment

To deploy a sandboxed environment, define a SandboxTemplate resource and keep pre-warmed Sandbox resources ready by using a SandboxWarmPool resource. You can then request a Sandbox resource from this warm pool by using a SandboxClaim resource. Alternatively, you can create a Sandbox resource directly, but this approach doesn't support warm pools.

SandboxTemplate, SandboxWarmPool, SandboxClaim, and Sandbox are Kubernetes custom resources.

Recommended: Create SandboxTemplate and SandboxWarmPool resources

The SandboxTemplate resource acts as a reusable blueprint. The SandboxWarmPool resource maintains a specified number of pre-warmed Sandbox resources with running Pods that are ready to be claimed. This warm pool reduces startup latency.

To deploy a sandboxed environment by creating SandboxTemplate and SandboxWarmPool resources, complete the following steps:

  1. In Cloud Shell, create a file named sandbox-template.yaml with the following content:

    apiVersion: extensions.agents.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: SandboxTemplate
metadata:
  name: python-runtime-template
  namespace: default
spec:
  podTemplate:
    metadata:
      labels:
        sandbox-type: python-runtime
    spec:
      runtimeClassName: gvisor # Required
      automountServiceAccountToken: false # Required
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true # Required
      nodeSelector:
        sandbox.gke.io/runtime: gvisor # Required
      tolerations:
      - key: "sandbox.gke.io/runtime"
        value: "gvisor"
        effect: "NoSchedule" # Required
      containers:
      - name: runtime
        image: registry.k8s.io/agent-sandbox/python-runtime-sandbox:v0.1.0
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8888
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "250m"
            memory: "512Mi"
          limits:
            cpu: "500m"
            memory: "1Gi" # Required
        securityContext:
          capabilities:
            drop: ["ALL"] # Required
      restartPolicy: OnFailure

  2. Apply the SandboxTemplate manifest:

    kubectl apply -f sandbox-template.yaml

  3. Create a file named sandbox-warmpool.yaml with the following content:

    apiVersion: extensions.agents.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: SandboxWarmPool
metadata:
  name: python-runtime-warmpool
  namespace: default
  labels:
    app: python-runtime-warmpool
spec:
  replicas: 2
  sandboxTemplateRef:
    # This must match the name of the SandboxTemplate.
    name: python-runtime-template

  4. Apply the SandboxWarmPool manifest:

    kubectl apply -f sandbox-warmpool.yaml

  5. Wait until the warm pool's Sandbox resources and their Pods are ready:

    kubectl wait sandboxwarmpool python-runtime-warmpool \
    --for=jsonpath='{.status.readyReplicas}'=2 \
    --timeout=600s

    If you create a SandboxClaim resource before the pool's Sandbox resources and their Pods are ready, the controller creates a new Sandbox resource for the claim instead of assigning one from the pool. In an Autopilot cluster, the Pods can take several minutes to become ready because GKE might need to create nodes for them.

Create a SandboxClaim resource

The SandboxClaim resource requests a Sandbox resource from the warm pool. Because you created a warm pool, the controller assigns a ready Sandbox resource (and its running Pod) from the pool to the claim instead of creating a new one.

To request a Sandbox resource from the warm pool by creating a SandboxClaim resource, complete the following steps:

  1. Create a file named sandbox-claim.yaml with the following content:

    apiVersion: extensions.agents.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: SandboxClaim
metadata:
  name: sandbox-claim
  namespace: default
spec:
  warmPoolRef:
    # This must match the name of the SandboxWarmPool.
    name: python-runtime-warmpool

  2. Apply the SandboxClaim manifest:

    kubectl apply -f sandbox-claim.yaml

  3. Verify that the Sandbox resource, claim, and warm pool are ready:

    kubectl get sandboxwarmpool,sandboxclaim,sandbox,pod

Alternative: Create a Sandbox resource directly

If you don't need the fast startup times provided by warm pools, you can deploy a Sandbox resource directly without using templates.

To deploy a sandboxed environment by creating a Sandbox resource directly, complete the following steps:

  1. Create a file named sandbox.yaml with the following content:

    apiVersion: agents.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Sandbox
metadata:
  name: sandbox-example-2
spec:
  podTemplate:
    metadata:
      labels:
        sandbox: sandbox-example
    spec:
      runtimeClassName: gvisor
      restartPolicy: OnFailure
      automountServiceAccountToken: false # Required
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true # Required
        runAsUser: 1000 # Required if image defaults to root (for example, busybox)
      nodeSelector:
        sandbox.gke.io/runtime: gvisor
      tolerations:
      - key: "sandbox.gke.io/runtime"
        value: "gvisor"
        effect: "NoSchedule" # Required
      containers:
      - name: my-container
        image: busybox
        command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
        args: ["sleep 3600000; echo 'Container finished successfully'; exit 0"]
        securityContext:
          capabilities:
            drop: ["ALL"] # Required
          allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
        resources:
          limits:
            cpu: "100m"
            memory: "128Mi" # Required

  2. Apply the Sandbox manifest:

    kubectl apply -f sandbox.yaml

  3. Verify that the Sandbox resource is running:

    kubectl get sandbox

Upgrade Agent Sandbox

To upgrade Agent Sandbox, apply the release manifest for the new version:

export AGENT_SANDBOX_VERSION="NEW_VERSION"
kubectl apply -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/releases/download/${AGENT_SANDBOX_VERSION}/sandbox-with-extensions.yaml

Replace NEW_VERSION with the version that you want to install, such as a version listed on the Agent Sandbox releases page.

Before you upgrade, review the release notes for the new version. If your cluster runs a version of Agent Sandbox earlier than 1.0.0, you must migrate your resources to the v1beta1 API before you upgrade, because version 1.0.0 removed the v1alpha1 API. For instructions, see the API migration guide.

If you deployed the Sandbox Router or applied the recommended security policy, repeat those steps for the new version.

Uninstall Agent Sandbox

Caution: Uninstalling Agent Sandbox deletes the Agent Sandbox CustomResourceDefinitions, which also deletes all Sandbox, SandboxTemplate, SandboxClaim, and SandboxWarmPool resources in all namespaces.

  1. Check for Agent Sandbox resources that are still in use:

    kubectl get sandboxes,sandboxclaims,sandboxwarmpools,sandboxtemplates \
    --all-namespaces

  2. If you applied the recommended security policy, delete the policy binding and the policy:

    kubectl delete validatingadmissionpolicybinding secure-sandbox-binding
kubectl delete validatingadmissionpolicy secure-sandbox-policy

  3. If you deployed the Sandbox Router, delete its cluster-wide RBAC resources:

    kubectl delete -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/${AGENT_SANDBOX_VERSION}/sandbox-router/deploy/rbac.yaml

    The router's other resources are in the agent-sandbox-system namespace, which the next step deletes.

  4. To delete the Agent Sandbox controller, its namespace, and its CustomResourceDefinitions, delete the release manifest for the version that you installed:

    kubectl delete -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/releases/download/${AGENT_SANDBOX_VERSION}/sandbox-with-extensions.yaml

Clean up resources

To avoid incurring charges to your Google Cloud account, delete the GKE cluster that you created.

gcloud container clusters delete ${CLUSTER_NAME} \
    --location=${LOCATION} \
    --quiet

If you created an Autopilot cluster, the location is the region (for example, us-central1). If you created a Standard cluster, the location is the zone (for example, us-central1-a).

What's next

  • Learn how to save and restore Agent Sandbox on GKE environments with Pod snapshots.
  • Learn how GKE Sandbox isolates workloads by using gVisor or microVMs.
  • Learn more about GKE security.
  • Explore the Agent Sandbox open-source project on GitHub.
  • Learn how to use open source Kata Containers with Agent Sandbox on GKE. Kata Containers isn't a Google Cloud product. If you install and use this software, then you're responsible for management and troubleshooting. Google's support and SLAs don't apply to Kata Containers.
